en: Preface to the Combined Commentary on the Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra:

Reading this single sūtra, "The Diamond," causes the conceptual mind to dissolve. This is because its principle is profound, its nature is detached, its practice is unattached, and its marks are non-marks.
Through these four aspects, which mutually illuminate one another, the text unfolds in a winding and repetitive manner until it ultimately returns [to the source].

It concerns nothing other than the absence of self, person, sentient being, or life-span. Yet, regarding the exhortation to uphold [this teaching] and the comparison of its merits, it is repeatedly and earnestly emphasized;

this is the general purport of the entire sutra. Thus one knows that this Prajñā is the unsurpassed secret seal, truly enabling people to realize the emptiness of nature (*dharmatā-śūnyatā*) and to dispel attachment to signs.
It is, for example, like a vajra, like a mass of fire, or like a blast of wind.
A hair-tip sword is like a pearl rolling on a plate; it is like trying to catch the wind or bind a shadow—uncontrollable and ungraspable. Such is the case.

Though many in the world recite and study these words, those who truly understand them are few. I, the ignorant one, have long lamented that the phrasing of this text is subtle while its meaning is profound;

though the metaphors are repeated, they are not redundant, and though the inquiries are frequent, they are not tedious. Indeed, even the composition of the *Sanlun* (Three Treatises) is increasingly difficult to comprehend, appearing almost as if—
In his commentary on the *Zhuangzi*, Guo Xiang took the commentaries to examine the text and used the text itself to verify the commentaries.

Where the commentaries were overly pedantic, he edited them; where their meaning was deficient, he supplemented them. Synthesizing these various commentaries, he formed a unified body of discourse titled the *Huìjiè* (Collected Explanations).
I have briefly set forth my limited views here to seek correction. Alas! Had one simply peeled away...

Its phrasing is already sufficient to dispel base avarice and untangle entanglements; how much more so when one attains the treatise through its exegesis, and realizes the sūtra through the treatise—how could it merely serve to eliminate [the literal meaning] as intended?
Written at the end of the pen on the full moon of the intercalary month in the year Xingwei of the Jiading era. By Baiting Shan Yue.
Preface to the *Combined Commentary on the Diamond Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Volume One.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Baiting Shan Yue of Siming.

The *Shilun xuanshi gangling* (Outline of the Preface to the Commentary) consists of four treatises in total: 1. *Jingang banruo boluomi jing lun* (Treatise on the Diamond Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra), three fascicles.
Composed by Bodhisattva Asaṅga; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta of India during the Sui dynasty.
2. A work with the same title as above, three fascicles. Composed by Bodhisattva Vasubandhu; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of Northern Wei.
3. *The Treatise on the Diamond Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra Entitled "Able to Sever"* (also in three fascicles).

Its verses are identical to those of the aforementioned commentary; this does not enter into the sūtra itself. Composed by Bodhisattva Asaṅga as verse, with a commentary by Bodhisattva Vasubandhu, translated by Tripiṭaka Master Yijing.
4. The title of the sūtra is the same as above: *Destroying Attachment While Not Destroying Conventional Designations*.
*Treatise in Two Volumes*. Composed by Bodhisattva Guṇadakṣa. Translated by the Śramaṇa Divākara of Central India.
Imperial Preface composed during the Tang Dynasty.

[Treatise] According to this, Asaṅga provides a comprehensive exposition of a single sutra through seven categories of meaning: first, the lineage is uninterrupted; second, the arousal [of the mind]...

1. The arising of the modes of activity (*ākāra*). 2. The locus where the three activities abide (these three are derived from a separate section of the sūtra). 3. The antidotes (*pratipakṣa*). 4. Non-loss (*avipraṇāśa*). 5. Determining the stages (*bhūmi-viniścaya*).
(Regarding the meaning of the general clarification: there are seven designations. (Although the names originally appear at the beginning of the treatise, they are established here from the end.

Among these, the first six demonstrate the ultimate fulfillment of the bodhisattva’s tasks, while the last one establishes this sūtra’s dharma-gate so that, as the seed of the Buddha, it may circulate in the world without interruption.

(This refers to establishing seven types of meaningful phrases based on the sūtra, and further establishing *prajñā* by means of those phrases. Furthermore, within the third stage of abiding, eighteen modes of abiding are opened up:

first, the arousal of the thought [of awakening] (*cittotpāda*) through to the eighteenth, the superior seeking of the Buddha-ground. (The enumeration of these names corresponds to the sūtra as follows). Moreover, they may be summarized into eight modes of abiding, which likewise suffice for fulfillment.

(The summary of the text is also complete): 1. The mode of abiding in inclusion; 2. The mode of abiding in purity; 3. The mode of abiding in aspiration; 4. The mode of abiding in freedom from obstacles.
(Compendium of the twelve kinds of obstacles within the aforementioned abidings: 5. Purification of the mind; 6. Culmination (corresponding to the sūtra as in the preceding abiding); 7. Vastness; 8.

Profundity (each of the preceding abidings possesses these two meanings). As stated in the section on the first abiding regarding how a bodhisattva should generate such a mind and so forth, this constitutes vastness.
Furthermore, it is said that if a bodhisattva practices giving without dwelling upon things, this is profound;
other cases of dwelling are explained by analogy (*etc.*). Regarding the four types of remedies: for each dwelling there are two kinds of remedies—first, wrong practice;

second, right practice accompanied by views (the treatise itself explains: "here, 'view' refers to conceptual discrimination"). If a bodhisattva should give rise to such a thought, this is the first [dwelling].

The antidote (is as follows): [it is said that] because ordinary beings are unable to give rise to such a mind, this serves as the antidote to their wrong practice. Furthermore, it is said that giving rise to such a mind is the wrong practice of a bodhisattva.

If a bodhisattva possesses the notion of a "sentient being" and so forth, this is immediately countered [by the following]. That is to say, if one gives rise to such a mind while maintaining a grasping notion, this is the wrong practice of a bodhisattva;

however, if it concerns the saving of sentient beings, this is a correct practice. Nevertheless, because it is accompanied by views, it is a correct practice that is shared with [wrong] views. This discriminative grasping must also be severed by the bodhisattva.

The remaining cases are explained by analogy. (Possessing both types of antidotes, it is from the beginning associated with *prajñā*). Regarding the "five non-losses," this refers to being free from the two extremes.

As it is said that there is both a "heap of merit" and a "non-heap of merit," this excludes the extreme of superimposition (*samāropa*), because one does not grasp at intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) within conventional discourse.
If it is said, "For this reason, the Tathāgata speaks of a 'mass of merit,'" this precludes the extreme of denial (*apavāda*).
Although it does not possess an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) as clung to by those verbal expressions, there is a referent that can be spoken of, because it was spoken by the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, if one says "Buddha-dharma" or "non-Buddha-dharma," this demonstrates the meaning of non-loss (*anapahāra*). If one says "this is called Buddha-dharma," this demonstrates the meaning of correspondence (*yoga*). Why?
This means that if one were to say that the Buddha-dharma possesses an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), the Tathāgata would not call it "Buddha-dharma";
this is the meaning of "not losing" [the truth]. Although he does not speak of it, one naturally knows that it lacks intrinsic nature;

this is the meaning of "correspondence. In this way, regarding the various stages (*vihāra*), two meanings are demonstrated: "not losing" (also called "unshared," meaning it is not shared with [wrong] views, yet carries the sense of not losing [the truth]; subsequent passages follow this pattern). 6. Determining the Stages.
These refer to the stage of practice through faith (*śraddhā-carita-bhūmi*), the stage of pure mind (*viśuddha-citta-bhūmi*), and the stage of the Tathāgata (*tathāgata-bhūmi*).

Among these, the first sixteen abodes constitute the stage of practice through faith; the abode of realizing the path constitutes the stage of pure mind; and the abode of seeking the Buddha-ground above constitutes the stage of the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, this [stage of the Tathāgata] possesses six [aspects], being endowed with the six kinds of purity and so forth. This corresponds to the expansion and contraction of the text regarding Vasubandhu’s "Dispelling Doubts" (*Vyākhyāyukti*). Seventh, the establishment of names (the text is as follows...).

Subsequently, by demonstrating the vastness and profundity in each instance, the essence of *prajñā* is revealed; next, by manifesting the non-loss of its remedies, the function of *prajñā* is disclosed.
Once both essence and function are made manifest, the principle is accordingly realized; and through such realization, one traverses the stages.
Only by traversing the successive stages does one reach the ultimate. Since this single scripture encompasses such vast and rich content, how could it be known without a treatise?

Verse: According to the commentary by the Tripitaka Master Yijing, the tradition of the Western Regions states that in the past, Bodhisattva Asaṅga personally received eighty verses of practice from the Venerable Maitreya in Tuṣita Heaven, which opened the gateway to the essential meaning of the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
(Some say that the Bodhisattva enters the *sūryaprabhā-samādhi* and ascends to Tuṣita, and so forth; this is the reason for the presence of verses in this sutra.
Next is the commentary by Vasubandhu (also called Sthiramati), which first establishes a precedent to resolve doubts, stating:

"From here below—that is, from the passage 'one should simply abide as instructed by one teacher'—all the sūtras manifest [the teaching] to resolve doubts. How do doubts arise? It is said that they arise from not abiding in the Dharma.
Regarding the practice of giving: how does one practice giving for the sake of the Buddha’s bodhi?

To sever such doubts, the text proceeds from the scriptural passage "as it is said" up until the subsequent verse, providing an exegesis through eighty stanzas. Within this, there is a sequential progression of themes.
The ancient commentary divided this into twenty-seven sections (though upon examination, the number of these divisions is not fixed, as seen later). This too is most excellent.

The essential purport of the entire scripture is exhausted [in these works]. However, the two translations (those of the Wei and Tang dynasties) differ slightly; there are variations regarding what is included in the sūtra and what is not.

Nevertheless, those that are included in the sūtra proceed in parallel with Asaṅga, and thus contain both the verses of the sūtra and their commentary. Those that are not included simply provide an explanation of the verse text and are termed "treatise-commentaries" (*śāstra-vyākhyā*).
This is what I recall being stated. Furthermore, the intention behind regarding the verse text as having been composed by Asaṅga follows the accounts of the tradition.
[It is also said to have been composed by the Bodhisattva Asaṅga (in Sanskrit, *Asaṅga*). ○ The *Puṇyavardhana-śāstra* subsumes the entire sutra under the meaning of the two truths (*satyadvaya*).
Thus, it states at the beginning: "All the teachings spoken by the Buddha converge upon the two truths.

The first is conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), which refers to the mutual connection between names, meanings, cognition, objects, karma, and its fruits, ranging from ordinary beings up to the Tathāgata. The second is ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), which refers to..."
The Dharma is ultimately unattainable. As it is said regarding the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), it is not within the sphere of cognition, much less that of words.
It is even devoid of karma and the fruits of karma; this is the lineage of the noble ones (*āryagotra*). For this reason, it is taught in this Prajñā that one does not abide in giving.
All phenomena are signless (*animitta*), and so forth, up to being without coming or going; this is the absolute truth (*satya*). Furthermore, it says:
All phenomena, mundane and supramundane, internal and external, as well as all their merits—this constitutes the establishment of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Since it does not transcend the two truths, the title is given as *The Treatise on Destroying Attachment while Not Destroying Provisional Names*.
The entire purport of this scripture lies herein. Examining its literary style and principles, although it differs slightly from the previous two treatises, nevertheless...
He dispelled doubts section by section, seemingly adhering to the ancient commentary of Vasubandhu; yet he cited it only sporadically, perhaps once or twice. What a pity!
I shall now collect them all together and provide a detailed explanation.
[The *Huìjiě*] says: This sūtra has six translations, and the treatise enumerates several schools of interpretation.

My current commentary relies primarily on the Qin version, as its text is concise, its principles are coherent, and it was the one most esteemed during that era. Nevertheless, the sūtras explained by the treatise vary according to their respective translations;

while they are largely the same, there are minor differences. Thus, when using those commentaries to explain this one, discrepancies and agreements inevitably arise. A comparative analysis follows below. Now, as for "non-... [the text continues].

As for Vasubandhu’s *Antarvyāptisamarthana*, its internal clarity is such that it has never differed from [the external]. Yet, while externally adapting to the requirements of the times, each work relies upon its own specific authority;
this is why the two treatises differ. Consequently, later generations find it difficult to follow them appropriately.

To adopt both simultaneously results in textual and semantic inconsistencies, making it truly difficult to synthesize them. To employ either one exclusively, however, leaves one unable to decide between their profound principles and subtle reasoning. Thus, based on these grounds...

Guifeng said: "To state that [the *Commentary on the Awakening of Faith*] 'dwells in eighteen locations to secretly reveal the stages of progression' and 'severs twenty-seven doubts to covertly connect the vital channels' is indeed well-said;
yet, its explanations are inconsistent. Although Qinglong’s sub-commentary attempts to harmonize these interpretations, Shibie refutes it.
As for Jingjue’s selections and omissions, they are perhaps biased; he maintains that severing doubts is the primary means of correctly explaining the meaning of the sutra."
To instead attach the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra* to the classification of Asaṅga is entirely to distort their teachings.

The recent work by Zhuan-an, which strictly follows Asaṅga while selectively adopting and rejecting Vasubandhu’s views, is even less a comprehensive treatise. Now, I maintain that both were holy masters.
How could one permit arbitrary acceptance or rejection? It is my view that Asaṅga had already composed the treatise (*śāstra*) before he heard the verses (*kārikā*).
How could it be permissible to suppress the treatise and fail to manifest it? Nor should it be appropriate to discard the verses and circulate them alone.

Therefore, they were transmitted to Vasubandhu so that he might provide an explanation; through this, we can discern his intention: to seek the ultimate truth in profound stillness and to assist in the transmission of the holy teachings. At first...

How could there be any discrepancy between these two? Furthermore, Vasubandhu received the teachings directly from Asaṅga, and Asaṅga received them face-to-face from the Compassionate Honored One (Maitreya).
Since the source and its current flow are unmixed, there can certainly be no error. Indeed, Asaṅga has already perfected the excellence of the structural divisions.

However, [the commentary] is brief regarding the structural progression (*utpatti*). Therefore, Vasubandhu further relies on the meaning of the verses to provide a comprehensive interpretation of the entire sūtra’s progression and resolve doubts, thereby detailing its exposition.
Now, in order to synthesize these, I shall first use Asaṅga to section the sūtra and rely on Vasubandhu for the structural progression;
I shall first list the various treatises appended beneath the sūtra, and subsequently present a harmonized commentary to supplement it.

I hope that by doing so, the words of the Sage will not be omitted and common parlance will not be intermingled, thereby manifesting the full excellence of these two treatises and establishing the characteristics of this single school’s interpretation.
[Sūtra] The Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra.
[Treatise] Asaṅga says: There are two meanings for the term "Vajra that can sever. First, "vajra" refers to being subtle and firm;

"subtle" means it is the cause of wisdom, and "firm" means it is indestructible. "Can sever" refers to what is severed through the hearing, reflection, and cultivation of *prajñā*, severing exactly where the vajra would cut.
It is also like the drawing of a vajra shape, which is wide at the beginning and end, but narrow in the middle.

"Narrow" refers to that which is narrow in the middle, namely the Stage of the Pure Mind (*śuddhacitta-bhūmi*). "Broad at the beginning and end" refers to the Stage of Faithful Practice (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*) and the Stage of the Tathāgata (*tathāgata-bhūmi*).
This demonstrates the meaning of the uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*). Regarding other treatises, there is no textual authority [to the contrary].

[Commentary] It is said: Names begin with the nameless; one attains the essence through names. One perceives the *prajñā* of ultimate reality (*bhūta-lakṣaṇa*) by means of the *prajñā* of words and letters.
This is why names are established. The title of this sutra is derived from its metaphorical dharma; the first two characters are the metaphor.
According to the treatise, it takes only "hardness" and "sharpness" as its meaning, referring to the nature of the *vajra* as being hard.
Therefore, it is indestructible; though refined a hundred times, its substance cannot be melted away. Because it is sharp, it can cut; thus, no myriad things can destroy its function.
It is commonly said in the world that only the *vajra* gemstone can be shattered; hence, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* refers to it as "gold-like *vajra*" in order to distinguish it [from the common gem].
Otherwise, those who do not know this may conflate the two into a single explanation, which is an error.
(As for the matter, it is explained separately. Now, "solid" (*kaṭhina*) is used as an analogy for the essence of *prajñā*, because it cannot be destroyed;
"sharp" (*tīkṣṇa*) is used as an analogy for the function of *prajñā*, because there is nothing it does not destroy. Furthermore, this treatise clarifies two meanings of the "Vajra":

first, "subtle," meaning it is minute, secret, and without interval, which can be compared to the causal wisdom of *prajñā*; second, "firm," meaning it is stable and indestructible, which can be compared to [the fruition].
Regarding the essence of the fruit of *prajñā*, it is simply called the "cause of wisdom" (*jñāna-hetu*); by citing the cause, one can understand the fruit.

Furthermore, that which "is able to sever" has two meanings: the first phrase refers to the dharma, taking the three types of wisdom (*tri-vidyā*) as that which severs; the second phrase refers to the metaphor, taking all delusions as that which is severed.
Alternatively, if one takes the meaning of gold’s brilliance and purity to metaphorically represent the three *prajñās*, such is the explanation.
This remains consistent with the general principle. Now that we rely upon the treatise, it is appropriate to explain it according to the original commentary.

Regarding the statement that the "diamond-drawn form" is narrow in its verbal expression, this refers to the fact that the stage of the Pure Ground (*śuddhabhūmi*) realizes only a single path. That it is broad at the beginning and end refers to the fact that the causal stage encompasses the myriad practices.
Because the fruit is endowed with all virtues, these are all explained in terms of the Bodhisattva stages; therefore, it is said that they "reveal the meaning of the uncommon.

Furthermore, within the gates of the teaching, there are both common and uncommon Prajñāpāramitās, as explained in the standard commentaries (etc.). The five characters beginning with "Prajñā" refer to the Dharma.
"Prajñā" is originally a designation for wisdom (*prajñā*); this fact that it is not translated [into Chinese] serves to manifest that its essence is sublime and supreme.

Therefore, as for "wisdom" (*prajñā*), there is nothing in either the mundane or supramundane realms that is not wisdom; thus, it would be insufficient to single out the wisdom of the present *Prajñāpāramitā*.
Furthermore, *pāramitā* is also a Sanskrit term; it is correctly translated as "reaching the other shore," or alternatively as "crossing over to the infinite."
"Ultimate accomplishment" (*kṛtaniṣṭhā*) and so forth are all translated according to their meaning; that is, the ultimate perfection (*pāramitā*) of reaching the other shore.
While these names apply generally to the preceding five perfections, they are derived specifically from Prajñā alone. To speak of them here serves to further clarify the ultimate meaning of Prajñā.
As for the sūtra, it is explained as usual (*etc.*). It is named thus because its essence is the ultimate reality.

Characteristics are thus cultivated; they take non-abiding as their ultimate principle and arise in dependence upon it. Their function is to shatter characteristics, and when surveyed, they constitute the teaching that universally constitutes Prajñā.
This is called the Mahāyāna vehicle—the teaching that harmonizes and sweeps away all characteristics.
There is nothing expounded by any single sutra that does not emerge from this principle; anything other than this is not [the truth].
[Sūtra] Thus have I heard... [omitted] ...having spread his seat, sat down. [Śāstra] Asanga said:

Regarding the body of the Sūtra, I shall now explain the meaning of its continuous succession of phrases. (This refers precisely to the five factors beginning with "Thus," which constitute the essence of a single sūtra.

Because this body of meaning causes the Prajñāpāramitā to circulate in the world, the lineage of the Buddha remains unbroken; this is the meaning of the phrase "continuous succession. For what reason did the World-Honored One, with a tranquil majesty...
He sat in the [proper] posture. This demonstrates that one who is solely tranquil is capable of awakening to and expounding the Dharma (awakening refers to the principle;

expounding refers to the teaching. It is not that he speaks only after having necessarily attained [realization]; rather, it signifies the meaning of being tranquil yet constantly illuminating). Regarding this, there is no text from Vasubandhu. Guṇaprabha says:
"Thus have I heard" indicates that this sūtra was expounded by the Bhagavat and was not composed by himself. "At one time" refers to when he spoke this...

Because the time [of this discourse] differs from other times, it specifies the location where it was taught, such as "in Śrāvastī," so that people may know this place where the Buddha once dwelt and planted the causes for merit.
Why are the assemblies listed at the beginning of all sūtras? To manifest the great majestic power (*mahā-tejas*) of the Tathāgata;
furthermore, it serves as a certification by the compilers (*saṃgītikāra*) that what they have transmitted is free from any divergent accounts.
[The *Huìjiě*] says: "All sūtras begin with these words; they are called the 'five matters preceding the sūtra' (*jing qian wu shi*).

Alternatively, they may be expanded into six, which are called the 'six accomplishments' (*liuchengjiu*). Because they serve as proof and inspiration for faith, they are termed the 'preface of proof and faith' (*zhèngxìn xù*), also known as the 'universal preface' (*tōngxù*) because it applies universally to all sūtras.
This is contrasted with the 'specific preface' (*biéxù') which belongs to this sūtra alone. The rest is as explained in the usual commentaries. It is also like...
The preceding treatise states: "At that time, the World-Honored One... and so forth; this is the specific introductory section. Begging for food is the standard, constant practice.

Now, however, it serves to initiate the giving characterized by non-abiding. Regarding the passage, "Having completed his sequential begging within the city, he returned to his original location," there is great significance.

Formerly, this was interpreted through the lens of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*) and other such methods (as detailed in the commentaries). Now, I shall provide a distinct explanation of its own. The City...

This serves as a metaphor for *nirvāṇa*. *Nirvāṇa* is the principle of primordial quiescence; it first emerges through non-emergence, and because one emerges with the knowledge of returning, one now returns and enters the city.
Begging for alms serves as a metaphor for the cultivation of the path (*mārga-bhāvanā*). The cultivation of the path is likewise a matter that is inherently present.
Now, one cultivates by means of non-cultivation. When cultivation reaches its ultimate limit, it arrives at the fruit. The fruit is the ground of ultimate nature;
therefore, one returns to the original place. By relying on this, one forgets conditions and purifies defilements, abiding in emptiness and ceasing all traces to demonstrate the Way.
This is why he gathered his robes and bowl, washed his feet, spread his seat, and sat down. Although these actions were performed by the Buddha, the principle should be applied to ordinary people;
thus, the underlying meaning is made manifest, and it is certainly not a mere formal ritual.
[Sūtra] At that time, the Elder Subhūti... [omitted] ...properly entrusts the bodhisattvas.

[Śāstra] Asaṅga says: Regarding the phrase "the single lineage is not severed" (hereafter the main teaching), it is for the purpose of clarifying the meaning that the Buddha-lineage shall remain unbroken in the future.
Therefore, Subhūti first addressed the Buddha, saying: "[The sūtra states: 'Excellent is the foremost gathering. This means:

Regarding the bodhisattvas who have already matured: when the Buddha, having attained enlightenment, turned the wheel of Dharma, he established seven kinds of great meanings for all bodhisattvas from among the first five meanings—excluding the determination of stages and the establishment of names from the seven types of semantic categories—as explained in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* and elsewhere.
These are well-comprised within what is beneficial and conducive to the welfare of bodhisattvas. Furthermore, they are called "foremost" by virtue of six kinds of meanings, namely:
"At one time" refers to up to six distinct periods; that is, because they skillfully encompass the dharmas of benefit and happiness for both the present and the future.

As for their differentiation, it is because they skillfully encompass the mundane dhyānas and the distinct vehicles of the Three Vehicles. As for their greatness and loftiness, it is because they encompass that which is unsurpassed.
It is "firm" because the Dharma is ultimate; it is "universal" because it universally encompasses both self and others;

it is "distinctive" because it excels among other bodhisattvas who have not yet attained purity. Regarding the "first entrustment," at the time of his parinirvāṇa, the Buddha likewise established the entrustment through five meanings:
to cause those who have already attained [the Dharma] to properly uphold it, and to cause those who have not yet attained it to do so as well. Furthermore...
There are six kinds of causal conditions: first, the entrance, which refers to being well-entrusted by a virtuous friend;

second, the nature of things (*dharmatā*), which refers to the Bodhisattva’s natural excellence in gathering [beings] through that very nature; third, the transmission of instruction, which refers to the fact that other Bodhisattvas should likewise take up the task of gathering them.
These demonstrate, in their respective order, the fulfillment of the six meanings: non-loss, compassion, and respect.
The lineage is not interrupted. The verse says (Maitreya):

One should know the meaning of skillful protection: Bestowing [the teaching] upon that body and practicing together; Not falling back from what has been attained and not failing to attain what has not yet been attained—this is called "skillful entrustment."

○ Vasubandhu’s Commentary (Wei Translation): This means that within the bodies of bodhisattvas who have already matured, it bestows the power of wisdom so that they may accomplish the Buddha-dharma (self-cultivation), and it also bestows the power of transformation so that they may gather in sentient beings (transforming others). This is the meaning of "acting in concert," which is termed "good protection.
Regarding those who do not fall back from what has been attained or what has not yet been attained: this refers to the virtues within bodhisattvas who have not yet matured.

There are those who have attained [the goal] and those who have not yet attained it; fearing they might fall back or lose what they have gained, [the Buddha] entrusts them to the wise so that they may attain non-retrogression.

Furthermore, this is for the sake of ensuring that those who have attained non-retrogression do not abandon the Mahāyāna, and for the sake of causing those who have not yet attained non-retrogression to advance further.
This is called "skillful entrustment. (The Tang translation states: "Skillful protection is the supreme benefit; through entrustment, one receives the commission. The rest is as before.
The text is largely the same. ○ Guṇadatta says: Among the various Mahāyāna sūtras, the virtues of the World-Honored One and others are explained at length;
because Subhūti has already given rise to pure faith, he says it is "rare. There are two kinds of protective mindfulness (*anuparigraha*): namely, true protective mindfulness.
The Tathāgata accepts them and causes them to awaken. The first is protective mindfulness, which causes the transformation of immeasurable sentient beings.
For what reason is this entrustment made? It is to praise and rejoice for those who have not yet seen reality, so that they may become the embodiment and form of a Tathāgata.
He entrusts them to the bodhisattvas to be looked after and protected; this also has two aspects: to cause the growth of those in whom the Buddha-dharma has already arisen.
It is for the sake of causing that which has not yet arisen to arise that he entrusts [the teaching] to them. For what reason does he praise only those who have not yet seen reality?
It is out of compassion for those who have not attained superior wisdom, so as to encourage and induce them to advance.
[The *Huìjiě*] says: "That an exclamation of rare wonder was uttered by the Tathāgata even before he had spoken—how profound its significance is!
It is just like when Subhūti sat in meditative seclusion within his cave, and Śakra, Lord of Devas, rained down flowers from the sky, and so forth."
By using that to manifest this, their essential intent coincides. This is like Subhūti and the Tathāgata reflecting one another in two mirrors;
within that, they expound the teaching with intense brilliance, and thus this praise is uttered. There is indeed a profound reason for this.
If this explanation were omitted, the words "rare" would merely be expressions of conventional praise. These have two meanings: first, [the meaning] has already been heard previously...
Because of the Buddha’s merits and the Prajñā previously described, there is this praise.
As in the preceding treatise, first, the subsequent question is initiated to serve as a point of discourse;

that is to say, the Tathāgata is able to protect and mindfully attend to all bodhisattvas through this Prajñā, so that they may achieve the perfection of their own practice. Furthermore, he entrusts these bodhisattvas with this Prajñā, so that...
Because his implements of transformation are complete, he acts with excellence and rarity, manifesting the supreme virtues of the Tathāgata.
Therefore, there arises the request as to how one should abide and how one should subdue the mind, in the hope that he will provide a definitive answer.
As for the fact that the treatise employs terms such as "three periods" and "the ripening or non-ripening of the faculties," these are likewise provisional clarifications;
ultimately, they reveal the excellent entrustment and the successive transmission of the teaching, thereby further demonstrating that the lineage of the Buddha remains unbroken.
[Sūtra] “World-Honored One, sons and daughters of good family who have resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* (omitted) wish to hear [this teaching].”
[Commentary] Asaṅga says: From here below is the second [section], the manifestation of the arousal of practice. There are six causes and conditions for Subhūti’s questioning:
first, to sever doubt (as explained by Vasubandhu in his *Vyākhyāyukti* on severing doubt, which likewise originates from this);

second, so that those who delight in merit may hear of its manifold virtues and thereby give rise to faith and understanding in the Prajñā; third, so that those who are already matured may enter into the profound meaning.
Fourth, it is for those who do not treat others with contempt, because they maintain [the teachings] through desire and do not regress.

Fifth, it is for those who have already attained compliant integration and a pure mind, so that they may enter into the Dharma and give rise to joy. Sixth, it is so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time in this and future lives;
it is also by means of Prajñā that the lineage of the Buddhas is made to remain unbroken. As the Sūtra asks, "How should one dwell?"—one should dwell [in this manner].
This refers to desire (*chanda*) and aspiration (*praṇidhāna*). "Desire" means seeking correctly; "aspiration" means forming a mental intention because there is something to be sought.
"Should practice" means that it corresponds to *samāpatti* (also called *samādhi*, etc.), which is non-conceptual meditative absorption.

"One who should subdue their mind" refers to the gathering and subduing of distraction; that is, when the mind is scattered during meditative concentration, one restrains it and causes it to return to its abiding state.
Furthermore, this sequentially reveals three kinds of paths: the path of gathering, the path of accomplishment, and the path of non-loss.
Regarding the three types of enlightenment, he asks specifically about the practice of the Bodhisattva Vehicle. Because his question is excellent, he is addressed with the words, "Excellent! (Sādhu).
[The second point] lacks textual evidence. Guṇadakṣa states: "That which is protected and remembered, entrusted to the bodhisattvas, and directed toward the Buddha-vehicle—how should one dwell?
Regarding "dwelling," it refers to in what kind of mark (lakṣaṇa) the mind of the fruit dwells. As for "aspiration" (*praṇidhāna*), it means:
what practice should the practitioner cultivate to obtain that fruit? As for "subduing" (*vinaya*), it means: what kind of mind should be subdued so that the cause becomes pure? All... [text ends].
In the Dharma, the cause comes first and the fruit later. Why, then, do you now first praise the virtues of the fruit? It is so that others may aspire to it with joy and thereby cultivate the causes.

"Listen attentively" means to focus the mind on a single object. "Well" (*sādhu*) means to give rise to faith in accordance with reality. "Reflect" means to respectfully uphold [the teaching] without forgetting.
"One should abide thus," and so forth, refers to abiding in such fruits and practicing such conduct in their respective order, thereby purifying [oneself].
Such a mind is, by its very nature, pure.
[The *Huìjiě* (Commentary) states: "When Kāśyapa was about to pose his question, he first said, 'A Bodhisattva who gives rise to this mind...
This is because for all who seek the Buddha-way, there is none that does not begin with this mind and conclude with this Way. To say it begins with this mind..."
This is the foundation from which [the practice] is initiated. That which culminates in this Way is the fruit one aspires to attain.

Therefore, in speaking of it, one first rectifies the foundation. This refers to the inquiry: "How should one dwell? and so forth. It means that if one gives rise to this mind, there must necessarily be a ground upon which to dwell.
To desire to dwell in a state of dwelling is logically impossible; for how could the mind characterized by marks of dwelling [be the true dwelling]?

It is indeed possible to accord with this. Therefore, one must necessarily subdue the mind. Thus, the subsequent passage stating that "one resolves the mind to save sentient beings without dwelling on signs" is the direct answer to this question.

Regarding the inclusion of the phrase "how does one practice" in the Wei translation while it is omitted in the Qin version, I maintain that each has its own intended meaning and need not be harmonized. However, even according to the Wei translation, although it speaks of these two...
There is external cultivation; only when it first attains correspondence (*saṃprayoga*) is it called "practice" (*caryā*). Thus, "correspondence" is used to explain "practice.

In the subsequent answer, however, the points do not roughly correspond, which seems to be incomplete (as seen in the later treatise). If one follows Kumārajīva’s translation, it states that both abiding and subduing constitute practice;
thus, the answer clarifies the question, and the phrasing and meaning are perfectly consistent. Therefore, one knows that the Qin edition is superior. Since the Buddha...
Xuanzang restated the question and said, "One should abide thus," and so forth. Some claim that these two phrases precisely demonstrate the profound essentials.

While this may indeed be the case for those of superior faculties who possess penetrating insight, it is generally understood as follows: the term "thus" (*evam*) is a direct expression pointing to the essence itself.
To perceive this is to realize the very essence of *prajñā*; it does not move even a single hair’s breadth. Thus...
[The text] remains thus. In this way, there is nothing that cannot be used to subdue the mind; however, the method for explaining the sūtras is not like that.
Since it says, "Certainly, World-Honored One, I wish to hear with joy," how could it be that Kongsheng was unable to understand this?

The commentators do not know this principle; one must explain according to the text and must not separately discourse on abstruse mysteries, thereby causing the logic and the phrasing [to become confused].
This is not appropriate. Therefore, we know that these two characters merely serve to indicate what is being explained.
[Treatise] Asaṅga says: From here below is the third section on the "places where one dwells," which concludes with eighteen gates throughout the sūtra.
First, the clarification of the arising [of the mind]. As in the sutra:
[Sutra] The Buddha told Subhūti: "All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas... (omitted)... are not, in fact, bodhisattvas."
[Treatise] Asaṅga says: When the Sūtra speaks of "all sentient beings," it is a general statement. When it speaks of those born from eggs and so forth, it is a specific statement.

There are three kinds of distinctions: first, the distinction of the modes of birth, such as being born from an egg; second, the distinction of the physical basis, such as having form (*rūpin*) and so forth;

third, the distinction of the objects encompassed, such as having perception (*saṃjñin*) and so forth. Regarding the phrase "I shall cause them all to enter nirvāṇa," for what reason is this vow made?

This meaning of "unattainability" (anupalabdhi) is without fault because it is subsumed under the category of "arising" (*utpāda*). That is to say, the emptiness of nirvāṇa is the meaning of unattainability;
all those sentient beings should be gathered by means of nirvāṇa so that they may emerge from birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*). Therefore, there is no fault—and indeed, no fault exceeding this meaning.

Since those born from eggs and the like are all included within the number of those who aspire [to liberation], they are all led into nirvāṇa, just as with the subtle classes such as those born from eggs or moisture, as well as those in difficult states such as the non-percipient beings (*asaṃjñin*).
How is it that they are all likewise led into nirvāṇa? There are three causes and conditions:

first, for those born in difficult places, they obtain the [right] time (for although they are born in difficult places, there are still those who attain deliverance at the proper time; some say this refers to "waiting for the time"). Second, for those not born in difficult places, they bring the immature to maturity.
Regarding those whose [karmic] ripening is already complete, because they are liberated, why not speak directly of *nirvāṇa* instead of saying "without remainder" (*anupadhiśeṣa*)?
This is because it is not distinct from the *nirvāṇa* attained through expedient means such as the first dhyāna; for that is obtained by one's own power and is not the ultimate fruit.

Why not say "with remainder" (*sopadhiśeṣa*)? Because that is a shared fruit, whereas this [latter state] arises from one's own past karma—meaning it coexists with afflictions and karma—and is not singular.
Regarding the body oriented toward the fruit: because suffering still remains (meaning the fruit of suffering has not been exhausted), there is no sentient being who attains nirvāṇa.
This is because, just as the Bodhisattva himself attains nirvāṇa, there is no separate sentient being [other than himself].

If a Bodhisattva possessed the notion of a "sentient being" (*sattva-saṃjñā*), such that he were to give rise to the notion of "another" (*para-saṃjñā*) toward sentient beings rather than the notion of their own self-nature (*ātma-saṃjñā*), then he would not be called a Bodhisattva. Therefore...

When afflictions give rise to the perception of sentient beings and so forth, the notion of a self arises. Because the Bodhisattva has already severed the view of a self, such perceptions do not arise toward them;

this is because they have attained the mark of equality in their own practice (the commentary notes that "practice" refers to the formations of the five aggregates). Furthermore, they resolve with faith upon the equality of self and others.
Moreover, when the Sūtra says that the Bodhisattva generates such a mind, it demonstrates the aspiration within abiding in this manner.
This is a prayer. If a bodhisattva possesses the notion of a sentient being (*sattva-saṃjñā*), they are not a bodhisattva.

Furthermore, when it says that if one gives rise to the notion of a sentient being and so forth, one is not called a bodhisattva, this demonstrates that during the practice of such correspondence, as well as at the time of subduing and gathering the distracted mind, there is no mark of a sentient being (*sattva-nimitta*).
This is because, at those times, the notion of a sentient being does not arise for the bodhisattva. As it is said:
Because he abides in the signs of the objects of knowledge (jñeya-lakṣaṇa) associated with that [realization], there is no sentient being who attains nirvāṇa.
The verse says:
The vast and foremost mind, That mind which is non-erroneous, Abides in the profound intention to benefit others.
Regarding the fulfillment of the merits of this vehicle, Vasubandhu’s commentary states: How does this verse explain how a bodhisattva dwells within the Great Vehicle?

It means that by means of four kinds of profound resolve (*adhyāśaya*), the bodhisattva dwells within the Great Vehicle with perfected merit. What are these four? First, the expansive mind (*vistīrṇa-citta*). Second...
First, the three constant minds and the fourth, non-perversion. As the sutra says, "generating such a mind," and so forth; this refers to the broad mind.
"Causing all to enter nirvana without remainder" and so forth refers to the first mind. "Thus delivering immeasurable sentient beings to extinction" and so forth [refers to the others].
This is the "constant mind. It means that because a bodhisattva regards all sentient beings as their own self, they never abandon or separate from them;

this is called the constant mind. When it says that a bodhisattva gives rise to the perception of sentient beings and so forth, this demonstrates the distancing from the signs of sentient beings based on the view of a self-body (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*);
thus, it is the non-perverted mind. [In the Tang translation, this is rendered as] the "profound mind" (*adhyāśaya*).
This constitutes the intention (*āśaya*). Among these, the first is the most excellent, and the constant mind is the ultimate. The remainder of the text is largely the same. ○ Guṇaprabha states:
"In this context, it is shown that the bodhisattva generates four kinds of corresponding minds; namely, the first is 'the boundless' (*ananta*)."
Second, the supreme; third, gathering through affection; fourth, correct knowledge. These correspond to the Sūtra as previously stated (*etc.*). Regarding "nirvāṇa without remainder":
it refers to the realization that all phenomena are by nature unarisen and empty, and the eternal cessation of all afflicted aggregates and so forth.
What is meant by "gathering through affection"? It means to love all sentient beings equally with oneself. If a Bodhisattva who has entered the stages perceives no sentient beings...

Furthermore, just as a stream-enterer does not give rise to the view of a self-existent body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and does not perceive even a single sentient being as "one whom I must deliver," how can this be called wisdom?
It is said that for one who has realized the true ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), the conceptualization of sentient beings and so forth will certainly not arise.

By the power of prajñā, although all things are ultimately unapprehendable, one abides in the mind by means of conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) and guides and delivers sentient beings through great compassion (mahākaruṇā).
[The *Huìjiě*] states: According to the questions posed, they are further specifically identified; logically, these should be answered with definitive judgments, yet Asaṅga...
The initial passage provides a direct explanation only. It is only from the section beginning with "Furthermore" (*punar-aparam*) that the three meanings are first displayed.
These appear to answer the three meanings within a single textual unit: namely, because one has accomplished those desires and vows, this is the meaning of abiding in the mind;

because one gathers the distracted through application, one does not turn toward the perception of sentient beings, which is the meaning of practicing subjugation. The text is already combined [with these points].

The explanation of the arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*) is concluded. The subsequent text is taken as the corresponding aspect of practice (*pratipatti*). Vasubandhu, however, uses the following text to answer the three questions (the text appears earlier and later).
The sequence of these [sections] differs from the current translation; both versions are difficult to reconcile regarding their pros and cons.

Now, it is said that those two treatises were translated by the same person. Since both are works of holy masters, it is not easy to pass judgment on them. One should consider that the meaning of the sutra is manifold and each [version] contains its own intent.
It would be appropriate to grasp their underlying principle. However, for now, following the Qin edition, one should adopt the commentary of Kumārajīva.
Thus, the first response concerns subduing (*vinaya*), and the second concerns abiding in the mind (*cittasthiti*); these can be understood from the headings and conclusions.

Although this slightly differs from the verses of the treatise, the principles of abiding in the mind and subduing are fundamentally compatible; therefore, there is no great harm. Now, "abiding" refers to abiding in the principle, while "subduing" refers to...
Subduing delusion and abiding in the mind are mutually dependent, yet they specifically achieve one another through a sequence of priority and posteriority. Question:

Since manifesting [the truth] arises from abiding and subsequently leads to subduing, why does the text first address abiding in the mind? Answer: It reveals that one must first achieve self-subdual and only then enter into abiding; therefore, it begins with subduing the mind.

Without first subduing the mind, there is no means to enter into the principle. Thus, the answer follows this sequence. Although this appears contrary [to the question], it is actually in accord [with the truth].

Thus, one should understand that answering "subduing" with "delivering sentient beings," and answering "abiding in the mind" with "practicing giving," is because the arousal of the bodhicitta is fundamentally based upon the Four Noble Truths, which have both general and specific aspects. Generally speaking, all four truths are the principles in which one abides.
Beneath each Truth, the arising of delusions is always possible; therefore, all must be subdued. Specifically, vows are based upon the Truths:
thus, the two vows for downward transformation take the salvation of sentient beings as primary, while the two vows for upward seeking take the cultivation of the Path as foremost.

I have specially sent this to indicate its essential point; there is indeed a reason for it. Thus, by entrusting the saving of sentient beings, one demonstrates the subduing of the mind, whereby both self and other are devoid of the notions of "self" and "person.
By entrusting the practice of giving, one demonstrates the abiding of the mind, whereby both cause and effect are devoid of any sign of dwelling.
Such being the case, the subduing [of the mind] primarily consists in the elimination of signs; it does not mean merely stopping at the act of saving sentient beings. Abiding...
The mind takes non-abiding as its primary focus; this does not mean being single-mindedly intent on the practice of giving alone, but rather proceeding directly in that manner.
One who can abide in such a way will necessarily be able to subdue [the mind] in such a way; the principle is one and the same.

However, when in accord with *prajñā*, there is nothing in which one does not abide and nothing that is not subdued. One must understand what constitutes accord and non-accord, and furthermore, observe their respective manifestations.
It simply abides in subduing [the afflictions]. This principle applies throughout the beginning and end of the entire sutra. Now, I shall explain it more directly.
When the sutra says, "I cause all to enter nirvana without remainder and attain extinction," it refers to the ten classes of sentient beings mentioned above.
One should deliver and liberate them all through the principle of the quiescence of *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*. Regarding the term "without remainder" (*nirupadhiśeṣa*):
in its proximate sense, it means that both the seeds and the fruits are exhausted, causing one to emerge from the triple world of segmented existence; this is called "without remainder.
Yet, according to the Great Teaching, in reality there is still a remainder. In its remote sense, it means that all are brought to extinction through the *parinirvāṇa* of the Tathāgata.

Only then can it be said that [nirvana] is ultimate and without remainder. Although they are thus extinguished, those sentient beings are fundamentally all quiescent, and there is no one who attains extinction.
The *Śāstra* explains this directly by means of "same essence" (*samavasthāna*), which captures its essential intent.
The three categories beginning with "immeasurable" may likewise be correlated with and explained according to the three aforementioned types of differentiated sentient beings. Why?

Therefore, the following section provides a detailed re-examination and explanation of the principle that, in reality, such things do not exist. This means that, as with the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), there is fundamentally no self or person;
thus, one does not perceive any sentient beings who could be saved. If one perceives them as existing, then there is "self" and "other.
Where there is self and other, there is selfhood and personhood; this is not what is meant by a bodhisattva in the present Prajñāpāramitā.
[Śāstra: Vasubandhu says: From here below, it is explained how a bodhisattva practices within the Mahāyāna and how they subdue their mind.
According to the Qin version, this immediately follows the answer to the question on "abiding in the mind" as set forth in the Sūtra.
[Sūtra] Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva should not dwell (or rest) upon any dharma; rather, they should be taught to dwell in this very manner.
[Śāstra] Asaṅga says: From here below is the second [section], the practice associated with the pāramitās, as well as that which follows within the various modes of dwelling.

Regarding "correspondence" (*yoga*), five types of explanations are given: first, based on meaning; second, the description of characteristics; third, sustaining; fourth, establishment; and fifth, manifestation.
In general, the antidote to various states of abiding is "based on meaning. That very state of abiding is the "description of characteristics.
Having desires and aspirations is "sustaining. Clarifying the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is "establishment. Gathering the distracted through correspondence is "manifestation. (General indication)
The Sūtra states that “a bodhisattva does not dwell in things,” and so forth; this is the basis for the meaning, as it reveals the antidote to dwelling in attachment.

When it says that “one should practice giving,” this explains the characteristic, meaning that the six pāramitās are also subsumed [within giving], because they all have the nature of *dāna* (giving)—that is, they all have non-attachment as their essential nature.
There are three kinds of *dāna*: first, the gift of material resources (*āmiṣadāna*); second, the gift of fearlessness (*abhayadāna*).

The three types of Dharma-giving correspond respectively to the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*). (As explained at length... Regarding these three kinds of Dharma-giving: if one lacks diligence (*vīrya*), one will become weary when preaching the Dharma;
if one lacks meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one will preach with a defiled mind, craving gain and offerings, and being unable to endure harassment and affliction.
If one lacks wisdom, such speech is perverted because it entails many faults. If one possesses all three [perfections], one achieves the gift of Dharma.

Furthermore, there are two kinds of fruits for the various pāramitās. The future fruit refers to how generosity (dāna) yields great rewards of merit, up to and including how wisdom (prajñā) yields sharp faculties and joyful bliss, due to attaining mastery among the assembly of great beings. The present fruit refers to—
Through *dāna* (generosity), one gains all forms of faith and respect; up to and including through *prajñā* (wisdom), one attains the bliss of the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma-sukha*) and so forth.

Among these, if one seeks future results, one practices giving while dwelling upon the objective thing (*vastu*), such as giving a gift and receiving a gift in return; the resulting retribution is limited and narrow.
If, as the Sūtras state, one practices giving and so forth without dwelling upon the objective thing, the results are manifold and cannot be specifically distinguished. If one seeks the present...
As for the fruit: it consists in abiding in form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and mental phenomena (*dharmas*).

If one says that giving is performed without abiding in form and so forth, this explains the grasping of the aspiration for giving. One who gives without abiding reveals the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) through such non-abiding;
they do not abide in any objective entities such as material objects. This is the establishment of the ultimate truth. Giving should be practiced in this manner.
"Not dwelling on the perception of marks" means that during the practice of samādhi and when gathering the scattered mind, one does not dwell on the perception of marks;
this is what is manifested. Furthermore, it is for the sake of enabling those who are unable to do so because they crave merit to become capable [of doing so].

(That is, by dwelling on marks to demonstrate non-dwelling,) the gift of non-dwelling on marks is revealed as having merit as vast as space. This is due to three meanings: namely, its pervasion of all places.
Second, vastness; third, inexhaustibility (and so forth). The verse says:
The meaning of *dāna* encompasses six [perfections]: Material goods, fearlessness, and the Dharma. Among these, the first, second, and third are called the "abodes of practice.
Regarding one's own person, repaying kindness, And the ripening of karmic fruit—none of these are clung to.
Having protected what one possesses, one does not give it away; one guards against seeking other matters.
Within those matters, one subdues the mind that grasps at signs and cuts off various doubts, while also guarding against the arising of a [rebirth-]producing mind.
Tianqin’s commentary states: "The meaning of *dāna* (giving) encompasses the six [perfections], meaning that all *pāramitās* are subsumed within *dāna*."
Because it manifests the meaning of the marks, "provisions for life" (*jīva-pariṣkāra*) is the actual name for the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*). Regarding the two types of fearlessness:
this refers to ethical discipline (*śīla*) and patience (*kṣānti*), which are also called *dāna*, because one does not give rise to fear regarding evil deeds already committed or yet to be committed.
Regarding the three types of Dharma-giving: this refers to diligence (*vīrya*) and the others, because one does not grow weary and knows the mind as it truly is when teaching. This is indeed bodhi—
This refers to the Bodhisattva’s dwelling in practice. Next, regarding the verse on "not clinging to one's own person," the Sūtra says:
"one does not dwell upon things. Regarding "not clinging to the repayment of kindness," the Sūtra says: "one should have no place of dwelling," which refers to offerings, veneration, and so forth.

Regarding "not clinging to karmic retribution," the Sūtra says: "one does not dwell upon form and so forth," which is precisely karmic retribution. Why, then, is it said that one "protects and preserves oneself" and so on?
That is to say, if one is attached to oneself, one cannot practice giving; if one seeks gratitude and the like, one abandons the Buddha’s bodhi.
These constitute the distinct meanings [of the faults]. To guard against these two, one remains unattached to all things.

Furthermore, the subsequent verse speaks of "subduing those objects," which means not perceiving the three factors of giving and so forth, as the sutra says: "one does not dwell on the perception of signs. Next, the benefits of giving are explained.
"Benefit. This means: if one were to be devoid of the conceptualization of the marks of giving and so forth, how could the merit of giving be accomplished?
To prevent such doubts from arising, it is taught that by not dwelling on the conceptualization of marks, the meaning of benefit is achieved. (The Tang translation states:

"In order to clarify that these also all possess the mark of giving, the one is subsumed within the six; that is, material giving is comprised by one, and the gift of fearlessness by two, while the gift of Dharma... )
Giving arises from three [factors]; these are the spheres of practice for the great bodhisattvas. As the sutra says, and so forth. The remaining text is largely the same. ○ Guṇadatta said:
"The three kinds of Dharma-giving are as follows: practicing with diligent effort without weariness; manifesting various supernormal powers;
and preaching the Dharma to others without grasping at anything. Furthermore, expounding and elucidating the various pāramitās for others—all these constitute Dharma-giving. Moreover...
Next, regarding "not abiding in things," this is explained in reference to the gift of material requisites (*āmiṣadāna*). One should not harbor attachment to the wealth being given;

for if one practices giving with craving, suffering will inevitably arise in the mind, or else one may later feel regret because of that gift. Regarding "not abiding," this is explained in reference to the gift of fearlessness (*abhayadāna*.
That is to say, when a bodhisattva cultivates ethical discipline (*śīla*) and patience (*kṣānti*), they should not give rise to a mind seeking the karmic fruit thereof. Not abiding—)

Regarding "form" (*rūpa*): this is explained according to the gift of Dharma (*dharmadāna*). The gift of Dharma has two fruits, because it relies upon the objects of the six sense-fields (*ṣaḍviṣaya*).

Yet, [the Bodhisattva] does not abide [in them], for when a Bodhisattva realizes ultimate reality (*tattva*), even the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) is not attained; how much less so the six sense-fields?

How does one practice giving so that the cause becomes pure? It means that all Bodhisattvas understand the gift of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) and do not harbor any conceptualizations regarding the gift or the object given.
Birth is the very subduing of the mind, by which it becomes pure. Some say: "There are three things, such as giving, from which a mass of merit can arise;
if these three factors are all forgotten, where would merit exist? This statement is erroneous, for it fails to understand the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Not dwelling in conceptualization, one practices giving according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*); such a mass of merit is difficult to measure, like [the waters of] the ten directions.
"Emptiness, etc.
[The *Huìjiě*] says: "While the Sūtra clarifies giving that is without abiding characteristics (*an-āśrita-lakṣaṇa*), the Treatise speaks of 'practices corresponding to the pāramitās.
It is precisely because of this non-abiding that they correspond. For Prajñā has non-abiding as its nature; non-abiding..."
Yet there is nowhere it does not abide. Therefore, by speaking of "non-abiding," all such characteristics are demolished;
by speaking of "nowhere not abiding," all these dharmas are established. This is thus abiding while not abiding, not abiding while abiding, and neither abiding nor not abiding.
Hence, the sūtra initially states: "One should have no place of abiding," and at the end it says: "But one should merely [act] like this..."

Regarding the abiding taught [in the scriptures], the characteristics are clarified through both definition and explanation; thus one knows that the statements of "abiding" and "non-abiding" have never been inconsistent.
Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Prajñā is like a mass of fire," which also means to take by way of non-taking.
The Wei translation speaks of three kinds of non-abiding: namely, practicing giving without abiding in things, practicing giving without abiding anywhere, and not abiding in form and so forth.

[The term] "giving" (*dāna*) and so forth are explained in various treatises and commentaries. Now, following the Qin edition, its meaning is one and the same; it refers to the heading of the initial passage.

That is to say, all phenomena are fundamentally characterized by emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Sentient beings, through deluded attachment, recognize them as existing and consequently give rise to clinging in every situation.
Therefore, [the Buddha] informs them that their nature is fundamentally non-abiding, so that they may practice in accordance with this truth. Thus it is said: "In..."

Because it is wisdom, it is said that "correctly teaching" means grasping in such a way that one can give rise to the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).

Therefore, when the Sūtra says "one should not grasp at dharmas," this does not mean grasping at dharmas according to their literal sound. Nor does "not grasping at dharmas" mean a mere absence of grasping; rather, it refers to the wisdom that accords with the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

To prevent this, it is said thus: "One who seeks offerings and honor" refers to a person who, desiring to receive offerings, praises themselves for possessing virtues such as moral discipline (*śīla*).

Furthermore, "one who produces" is so called because they are the cause that gives rise [to results]; "one who grasps" is so called because they perfume and cultivate the fruit of their own continuum (*sva-ātmabhāva*).

Therefore, regarding the statement, "If one grasps at the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), one becomes attached to a self (*ātman*) and so forth," this means that while there may be only the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of ignorance (*avidyā*) and no manifest coarse afflictions (*paryavasthāna*), there is still the grasping at a self (*ātmagrāha*) despite the absence of the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*).

This is because the raft metaphor (*kolopama-dharmaparyāya*) states that these teachings are to be abandoned, not that the Dharma itself is to be abandoned. The verse says, "They do not abide in following [the teachings]," which demonstrates the realization within the Sūtra teachings.
Wisdom does not abide, because one who has attained realized wisdom abandons all phenomena, just as one who has reached the far shore discards the raft.

Because it is an action conducive to the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*), it is able to lead toward the three types of ethical discipline and toward the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).

Because they are unarisen, they are also without cessation; therefore, there is no perception of non-dharmas.
Since one is free from the discrimination between dharma and non-dharma, there is no perception. This statement that "there is no perception" merely reveals the absence of perception.

It is not that there is no phenomenon and thus it is called "non-perception. Although the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is free from all conceptualization, because it conforms to worldly discourse, it is also not "without perception.

Regarding the inclusion of the term "precept-merit" alongside "wisdom," the treatise indeed addresses this. First, it is to manifest the distinct meanings of the characteristics of that which can be believed;
as Vasubandhu [states]. Second, it is because all merits are subsumed herein; as Guṇadatta [states].

Furthermore, one may possess precept-merit alone, yet despite having faith, lack understanding; or one may possess wisdom alone, yet despite having understanding, it is not necessarily [accompanied by merit].

Faith. It is only when the three virtues are complete that one attains faith and understanding; this refers to what is called "conditions being able to assist realization" and "realization being able to give rise to the correct [view].
Now, the Qin version omits the word "able" (能), while the Master Zhi’s intention is to include it as part of the chapter title.
Although the scripture speaks of either "the final five hundred years" or "the final fifty years," and thus admits two interpretations, we take the Qin version as authoritative. This is because...
Regarding this "reality": faith is the reality of realities; it does not mean [the thing itself] is real. The discourse on knowledge and vision has been explained in detail.
It is free from such things as the mark of a self (*ātman*). The fundamental basis for being able to believe is precisely this: it is rooted in non-self (*anātman*).
To have a self is to contradict *prajñā*; therefore, one cannot believe. This is why it is profound, pure, and the means by which merit is attained.
"Immeasurable" means because of non-self. Thus, that which the Tathāgata knows and perceives does not refer to knowing a self;
rather, he knows its absence of self. It is the same for what he sees. Not only do the Buddhas perceive sentient beings therein, but sentient beings also perceive the Buddhas therein.
One should know that the ultimate limit of the mark of a self is the ultimate limit of non-existence.
The self and non-self reach their ultimate limit in *prajñā*. Within *prajñā*, all knowledge, vision, faith, and understanding arise from non-self;
how can one fail to investigate their origin? In this treatise, two sets of four characteristics are clarified. Regarding the four characteristics of the "self" (some say:

the notion of a self, the notion of a sentient being, the notion of a life-span, and the notion of seeking further rebirth; others say: the notion of a self, the notion of a living being, the notion of a soul, and the notion of a life-span—the sources differ and the terminology varies), we now rely upon [the following]:

The Qin school fundamentally takes the self (ātman), person (pudgala), sentient beings (sattva), and life-span/individuality (jīva) as its sequence and its orthodoxy—the verse mentions "life-span" and so forth because they are listed last). They are also called the four views, the four attachments, the four graspings, and so on;

in full, there should be sixteen types of views regarding the self and person (*ātma-pudgala-dṛṣṭi*). (For details, see the *Fajie Cidi* [Graded Sequence of the Dharma Realm] and the commentary on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, etc.).

Nevertheless, all of these arise from the real dharmas of the aggregates, bases, and elements, taking the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) as their root; according to what is grasped and conceptualized, one attains [these various designations].

The names differ—four and sixteen—through the opening and closing of their designations (and so forth). While various treatises provide detailed explanations of these meanings, they are not lacking in thoroughness;
nevertheless, I shall now explain them further according to common understanding. Now, phenomena (*dharma*) are fundamentally without self (*anātman*).

That which is perceived as a sovereign master is the "self" (*ātman*). This is what is meant by the self: that humans are more spiritual than wood or earth, and that their nature is immutable. This is, for example, like...

The "person" exists within the person. That which is born from the fundamental four great elements and the five aggregates as a collection of dharmas, yet grasps them as its own possession, is the "sentient being.
That which maintains impermanent dharmas as permanent is the "life-span. By analogy, other explanations may also be understood accordingly.
Regarding the fourth [section], the "Characteristics of Dharmas," the Wei translation contains both an enumeration and an explanation; the enumeration follows first.

Establishing [the teaching] through subsequent negation (*dàng*), it is said that "the characteristics of dharmas are one and equal. The explanation follows the sutra; for instance, it says, "there are no characteristics of dharmas, yet it is not the case that there are no characteristics of dharmas.
Thus, by means of two layers of negation and establishment, four characteristics are formed. Although they appear in a sequence, in principle there is no contradiction.

When it is said that "dharmas exist" while "characteristics are absent," this refers to speaking of the nature (*xing*) by way of the characteristics (*xiang*). When it is said that "emptiness truly exists," this refers to emptiness itself.
Fundamentally there are no things; this is what is meant by "nature" when speaking of "characteristics. Therefore, the characteristic of emptiness is precisely existence.

Furthermore, regarding the statement that "those [things] are empty and non-existent, yet these cannot be said to be either existent or non-existent," it means that those are called "empty" only in reference to their characteristics; thus, emptiness itself is not inherently empty.

Because there is no entity, characteristics are themselves emptiness; thus, characteristics are also non-characteristics. These are spoken of in relation to one another and cannot be described in terms of existence or non-existence.
Since both these characteristics and non-characteristics are empty, they are called "non-characteristic. To speak by way of this:

first, [the teaching] relies on the relative opposition of the two extremes of emptiness and existence; subsequently, it relies on the relative opposition of the absence of both emptiness and existence. Thus is the discourse.
As for "characteristics," their meaning lies in the Middle Way. Since one has already abandoned all four extremes, even this "middle" is not established;
this is what is meant by saying that the Middle Way does not require being posited. Now, the Qin version abbreviates and combines these points, stating simply:

"There is no mark of dharmas, nor is there any mark of non-dharmas. This precisely relies on the simultaneous clearing away of both emptiness and existence to directly reveal the Middle Way. Thus, it is Prajñā.
The purport of destroying marks (*lakṣaṇa*) is thus made manifest. Although each [commentary] has its own reasoning, Kumārajīva’s is concise and superior.

Regarding the passage beginning with "For what reason," [Vasubandhu] relies on Asanga to refute false grasping and accordingly explains the text; since [Asanga] has already clarified that both [self and dharmas] are abandoned, Vasubandhu conversely elucidates his own position.
Now, following the Qin edition, I shall provide a direct explanation. This is precisely because the preceding statement said there is no longer any mark of self (*ātman*).
Furthermore, it is said that there are no characteristics of dharmas (*dharmalakṣaṇa*). Therefore, the meaning of this retrospective clarification through negation is explained again:
if the mind grasps at characteristics, this is the mark of self (*ātman*). Where there is the mark of self, there is grasping for a self (*ātmagrāha*).

Whatever takes up the characteristics of dharmas or the characteristics of non-dharmas, all such instances inevitably involve attachment to self and person (*pudgala*). Thus, there are three successive stages of dispelling attachment, and furthermore—

It merely issues forth the two kinds of emptiness. That is to say, the first [stage] proceeds from the real toward the conventional, which is the emptiness of persons and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-śūnyatā*).
The second proceeds by means of both phenomena and non-phenomena, which is the emptiness of intrinsic nature and characteristics (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*).

Therefore, it is explicitly concluded: "For this reason, one should not grasp at dharmas," and so forth. Since nothing is grasped, there is nothing that is not eliminated; thus, the ultimate emptiness of the Middle Way is clarified. However...
If so, how can it still be said that the Middle Way is preserved? It is said: The essence of the Middle is fundamentally detached; therefore, it should neither be discarded nor established.

Nevertheless, when it is said to be "discarded," one discards only the attachment to emotional states. As for the statement that there are five types of erroneous grasping due to the lack of attachment:

this is because the [text] generally refutes the conceptualization of reality. The Sūtra speaks only of the transformation of the concepts of "dharma" and "non-dharma"; these refer to the internal dharmas and the two types of ordinary persons.
Because bodhisattvas who harbor pride regarding their vehicle and so forth still possess views that cling to the characteristics of phenomena and non-phenomena, this is discussed here.

As for other notions such as the "self-conception" (*ātma-saṃjñā*) and so on, these are attachments held by non-Buddhists; furthermore, they involve the transition between perception and non-perception, and thus are not the essential points to be refuted in this text, so they are set aside and not mentioned.
It further states: "However, regarding the self-conception, those latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) that have not been severed... This, moreover—
Regarding the discussion of coarseness and subtlety within the notion of self (*ātman-saṃjñā*): it refers to one who has already severed manifest afflictions (*kleśa*).

Although such a person lacks coarse notions, because their latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) have not been severed, they transform into the grasping of a self (*ātma-grāha*), thereby grasping at the notions of "dharma" and "non-dharma.

This, too, is merely the notion of self. (The text uses the term *anuśaya*; Vasubandhu explains this in contrast to manifest, coarse delusions, which is precisely ignorance [*avidyā*]). This refers to other meanings contained within the transformation of this notion of self.
The sutra has not yet explained this. Whether these [terms] are general or specific, or whether they progress or regress, the text is somewhat difficult to clarify.

I shall therefore elaborate upon it. Under the "raft simile" dharma-gate, the citation of analogies serves as proof. Regarding the meaning of "dharma" and "non-dharma," as explained in various treatises, there is nothing that is not correct.
It may also be said that "non-dharma" refers to *prajñā*. As for all the characteristics of dharmas, one must still...
