[The Doubt]: The following section serves to dispel a different doubt. Previously, it was stated that the Tathāgata cannot be seen by means of the accomplishment of marks.
For what reason, then, is Śākyamuni called a "Buddha" upon attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and how does he further preach the Dharma?
To sever this doubt, [the sūtra] says as follows.
[Sūtra] Subhūti, what do you think? Has the Tathāgata attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
(Omitting the intervening text) It is not, indeed, the Buddha-dharma.

[Śāstra] Asaṅga says: What follows here clarifies the realization of the Dharmakāya, which is further twofold: first, the aspect of wisdom (jñāna-lakṣaṇa); second, the aspect of merit (puṇya-lakṣaṇa).
Regarding the aspect of wisdom that attains the Dharmakāya, the Sūtra speaks of the Tathāgata attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and so forth.

This is shown according to the meaning in order to overturn [the notion of] "perfect enlightenment" (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) as a grasped object, and because all dharmas taught therein are ultimately unapprehendable (*anupalabdha*).
Therefore, it is said that there is no fixed dharma; this is Subhūti’s way of conveying the Buddha’s intention.

If one were to say that there is a dharma that can be explained and named "bodhi," this would be a description of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). It is for the sake of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) that bodhi and its attainment are spoken of as existing;

this is done with the desire to provide encouragement and support through skillful means (*upāya*). If one acts according to the Buddha’s intention, then both [the existence of bodhi and its attainment] are absent. Hence it is said: "As I..."
Regarding the passage beginning with "understanding what the Buddha has taught," and further stating that "all dharmas taught by the Tathāgata are ineffable" and so forth:

"taking" refers to the time of correctly hearing [the teaching], while "speaking" refers to the time of expounding it. Because of this speaking, one knows that both the act of speaking and that which is spoken are both ungraspable.

This is precisely the establishment of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). It is not "dharma" because it is of the nature of conceptual differentiation (*parikalpita-svabhāva*); it is not "non-dharma" because of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*).
As for being called a "sage" by virtue of being unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*): if the meaning of non-conceptualization is what is termed "unconditioned," [then this applies].
This bodhisattva is designated by the name "one in training" (*śaikṣa*), because they manifest the integration of the concentrated and the distracted states.

If the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) of the Tathāgata—being without arising and without activity—is called "unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*), then the Tathāgata is designated by the name "one beyond training" (*aśaikṣa*), for he is the supreme awakening of the ultimate truth alone.
Next, regarding the statement that the marks of merit lead to the attainment of the Dharma-body, the Sūtra says: "If a person were to fill..."
In a world-system as vast as the trichiliocosm, the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata’s marks of merit arises from that very teaching of the Dharma-body.
Even a single four-line verse produces immense merit; how much more so, then, the entire mass of the Tathāgata’s marks of merit!
To establish this meaning, it is said that the Tathāgata’s *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* arises from this, through the universal practice of the ten dharma-activities.

Because it is inclusive. (The ten dharma-practices have not yet been examined. Furthermore, it is by virtue of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) that one speaks of the Buddha’s birth and his attainment of *bodhi*.

These two are both designated as "Buddha-dharmas. It is further said that the Buddha-dharmas are themselves not Buddha-dharmas. Moreover, regarding the statement that the merit produced [by this] surpasses that [other] merit:
because it relies on the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*), it reveals the counteractive [nature] whereby merit does not arise; therefore, it is said that its merit is [in fact] non-existent.

It is said that their characteristics are superior to those [of ordinary beings], being sustained by desire and aspiration. This accumulation of merit is, in fact, not an accumulation of merit, nor is it the Buddha-dharma, and so forth;
this collectively reveals the establishment of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), for it is designated as such because it accords with the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
The inclusion of the distracted through correspondence is no longer further elucidated. (The first fascicle ends here). The verse says:
The emanation is not the true Buddha, nor is it the speaker of the Dharma. In teaching the Dharma, there is no dualistic grasping;
it is without speech and free from the characteristics of words. Both the one who receives and upholds [the teaching] and the one who speaks it are not devoid of merit.
Yet merit alone does not lead to Bodhi; only these two can lead to Bodhi. Regarding reality, they are called the "causes of realization."
It also serves as the cause for other births; Only the Buddhas’ dharmas Bring about the supreme essence of merit.

Tianqin’s commentary states: There are three kinds of Buddhas: first, the Dharma-Buddha; second, the Reward-Buddha; and third, the Transformation-Buddha. The present Śākyamuni is a Transformation-Buddha.
He neither realizes *bodhi* nor preaches the Dharma, just as the sutra says there is no fixed dharma.
Therefore, it is not the case that he does not speak at all. To preclude this [misunderstanding], it is said: "He teaches the Dharma without dualistic grasping.
This means that it is not that he does not speak; rather, it is because the speaker and the listener do not grasp at either dharma or non-dharma.

This is because those dharmas, non-dharmas, and non-non-dharmas are taught in accordance with the meaning of *tathatā* (suchness). As for "non-dharma," it is because all dharmas lack intrinsic essence and characteristics. It is not "non-non-dharma" [in the sense of being nothing at all].
This is because that True Suchness (tathatā) truly exists as the characteristic of selflessness. Why, then, is it said that one speaks but does not realize?
It is because when there is speaking, it constitutes the meaning of realization; if one were not realizing, one would be unable to speak. As the Sūtra says:
"All noble ones (ārya) are named by means of unconditioned dharmas (asaṃskṛta-dharma)," because those dharmas are the cause for their speaking. All noble ones rely upon the dharma of True Suchness.
Therefore, one is able to speak of those unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharmas. For what reason, then, is it said that those dharmas are ineffable?
All the more so regarding such grasping; for they are free from the characteristics of verbal expression and are not objects that can be spoken of.

As for the term "all noble ones" (*ārya*), it is because they possess a portion and a full realization of *tathatā*. Furthermore, the sūtra speaks of a comparison of the merit of giving the seven treasures by means of a parable.
Although the Dharma is ineffable, it is grasped, and thus its merit is not empty. Therefore, the verse says [as follows].

Regarding the statement that "merit does not lead to Bodhi" and so forth, this means that both upholding and expounding can lead to Bodhi, as in the sūtra passage beginning with "upholding even a four-line verse.
This phrase "mass of merit" has two meanings: first, the sense of accumulation; second, the sense of proceeding toward [enlightenment].

[The commentary on] the meaning (*artha*) states: (The *Śāstra* [Treatise] says "the meaning of accumulation" (*puñja-artha*), but this is twofold; the phrasing seems not yet settled and is also too brief. It should rather say: "The phrase 'heap of merit' (*puṇya-puñja*) has two meanings, namely: heap and non-heap. The verse also has two meanings, namely: approaching (*gati*) and non-approaching.

Matching the verse to the Sūtra, 'heap' is non-approaching, while 'approaching' is non-heap—these are the only two meanings. Therefore it is said: Just as a person carrying a heavy burden cannot proceed forward, so too that heap of merit, because of its accumulated weight, cannot proceed toward Bodhi;
it is for this reason called a "heap. It is not a "heap of merit" [in the sense of being a true accumulation].
This is because it is capable of leading to both [results]; thus, it is superior among all merits. As for why it is capable of leading, it is as the sutra says:
"The bodhi of all Buddhas is born from this very sutra," and so forth. Therefore, the verse states: "Regarding reality, it is called the revealing cause."
That which is called *bodhi* is termed the *dharmakāya*. Its essence is truly unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). These two [merit and wisdom] serve as the causes of comprehension for it.
Although they do not act as the cause for birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), they nevertheless serve as the cause for *bodhi* for the other two Buddhas—the *nirmāṇakāya* and the *saṃbhogakāya*.
Thus, this is the unique quality of all Buddhas alone; because this merit can accomplish that supreme, uncommon essence, it is thus called "merit."

The virtue is great. ○ According to the Tang translation, "shoulder" (aṃsa) is further interpreted as having the meaning of "advancing" (prasthāna), because that which is on the shoulder is able to bear [the load].

Thus, this collection of names is designated as the "shoulder," whereas that which cannot bear [the load] is defined as not being a "collection" (skandha), and so forth; in this way, the explanation is inverted.

The first point is the loss of principle; the remaining text is largely the same. Guṇadakṣa says: This clarifies that when the Buddha realizes the ultimate reality, there is no dharma that can be grasped.
To speak of "expounding the Dharma" is to conform to conventional designations and names; it is not the primary truth (*paramārtha*).
Because neither dharma nor non-dharma is grasped, it is called *bodhi*. As for saying that the Buddhas realize *bodhi*, it means realizing through non-attainment.
Because awakening is unborn, Subhūti answered with intentional meaning that there is not even the slightest dharma to be apprehended.
This does not mean that he has failed to realize the unborn through direct perception. When he says it is "ungraspable and inexpressible," it is because there is no grasper and no speaker.
"Unconditioned" means the sense of non-apprehension. "Noble ones" are those who perceive the true reality. "Speaking for others" refers to...

This means that because he is able to skillfully expound the two truths without error, his merit surpasses that [of others]. This is due to two gates: namely, principle (*nyāya*) and teaching (*śāsana*).
Regarding the teaching, the Sūtra says: "The foremost among all forms of giving is the gift of Dharma (*dharmadāna*)," because other material gifts (*āmiṣadāna*) are subsumed within it.
Regarding the principle, material gifts lead one to remain within *saṃsāra*, whereas the gift of Dharma can accomplish ultimate merit. Thus said the Buddha.
That "dharmas are not the Buddha-dharma" means that the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of all dharmas is empty and non-existent.

If one were to manifest this [emptiness] as the Buddha’s Dharma-body while still perceiving it as having an intrinsic nature, one has not yet awakened to the dharmas. It is with this underlying intention (*saṃdhi*) that it is said they are "not the Buddha-dharma.

If one knows that dharmas lack intrinsic nature and realizes this, one is called a Buddha. If one upholds these dharmas while understanding them to be without intrinsic nature, this is called the gift of Dharma (*dharmadāna*).
(3. Dispelling Doubts). [The *Huìjiě*] states:

Because it can be clearly explained, it is said to be of two kinds. Regarding the Sūtra’s statement that there is no fixed dharma, Śūnyatāgarbha profoundly grasped the Buddha’s intention, meaning that what is attained and what is taught has no definitive meaning; this is also what is called the inconceivable.
He then explained it himself, saying: "All are ungraspable and unspeakable; they are neither dharmas nor non-dharmas," and so forth. This means that these dharmas are subtle and wondrous.
Because they can be mutually attained, it is said that they "cannot be grasped. Because principle cannot be demonstrated through words, it is said that it "cannot be spoken of.
When one refers to its "Dharma-nature," its essence is unattainable; when one refers to it as "non-Dharma," its characteristics are substantially existent.

Because this is explained in reliance upon True Suchness (*tathatā*) and the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), it is said to be "neither Dharma nor non-Dharma. Furthermore, it is said that all worthies and sages...
It is further explained that there are distinctions within unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*). All the teachings mentioned above arise by depending upon unconditioned phenomena;
such is their explanation. This is precisely another name for *tathatā* (suchness), yet there are distinctions [within it].
It is not that there is no distinction within the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); rather, it is precisely because of the distinctions among those who rely upon it [the unconditioned] that such is said.
The Wei translation states: "Those named 'Worthy and Holy' refers to all worthies and sages. It is because they all take the unconditioned dharma as their basis that there are degrees of depth;

thus, the titles of 'sage' and 'worthy' are established, and this is the reason for the difference between those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). The verse says: "The response-body and transformation-body are not..."
The true Buddha is likewise not the one who preaches the Dharma; that which is called Śākyamuni is a manifested transformation (nirmāṇakāya).
That which cannot be seen through physical marks is the true Buddha. These two cannot be discussed as being on the same level; this is the intent for severing doubt.

As for the statement that "the transformation Buddha does not realize bodhi, nor does he preach the Dharma," this is spoken from the perspective of subsuming the Dharma-body and Reward-body into a single provisional discourse.
Nevertheless, it is not that one attains bodhi without preaching the Dharma; rather, because there is no fixed dharma, one attains yet does not attain, and preaches yet does not preach.
Master Zhao said: "The various marks dazzle the eyes yet are not forms; the eight tones fill the ears yet are not sounds.
Furthermore, if one distinguishes by means of the three bodies, it is the Sambhogakāya Buddha who attains bodhi.
The preacher of the Dharma is the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body). That which is without preaching and without attainment is the *dharmakāya* (dharma body).

If one explains them as being identical, then the *nirmāṇakāya* is itself the *dharmakāya* and the *saṃbhogakāya* (reward body); thus, there is attainment yet no attainment. Since the *dharmakāya* and the *saṃbhogakāya* are themselves the *nirmāṇakāya*, there is preaching yet no preaching.
Each has its own intended meaning, and the principle must not be viewed in a partial manner. Next, regarding the *dharmakāya* with its marks of merit, first an analogy is presented for comparison.
Regarding the measure: as for saying "very much," although it is much in terms of the phenomena involved, it is inferior when compared by way of the Dharma;

therefore, it is said that "this merit is not the nature of merit. Thus, when the Tathāgata says the merit is much, he speaks of "much" merely as a provisional answer in accordance with the phenomena.
It is not because the nature of merit is "much" that he uses the word "much"; rather, if one looks toward the merit to be compared in the subsequent passage, this [present merit] is merely...
Regarding "merit," it does not by itself lead to Bodhi; this is why the Qin edition specifically adds the character for "nature" (性).
The intent is that the subsequent text clarifies that the merit of upholding the sutra is superior, namely that these two [types of merit] can lead to Bodhi.

As for the passage beginning with "For what reason," it further interrogates and explains the sense of its superiority over those [other merits], because it can give rise to both Bodhi and the Dharma-body. Now...
The translation is abbreviated; it simply says "emerges" (*niḥsṛta*) rather than "is born" (*jāta*), as the meaning encompasses both. However, that which emerges is the Buddha-dharma.
Since the Buddha-dharma is not [a fixed] dharma, one fears that even this might become an attachment;
thus, one must even abandon views regarding the Buddha-dharma, let alone other dharmas. This statement of negation is used by various treatises to establish the primary [truth].

Exegesis of the Meaning: It may be explained in terms of realization, or it may be explained by means of "the absence of intrinsic nature" (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) and so forth; each approach possesses its own logic, as can be understood through careful examination.
[Doubt]: Vasubandhu says: Regarding what was previously stated—that the noble ones speak of the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) as being ungraspable—[this applies to] the *srotāpanna*...
The [Stream-enterer] and others also take up their own fruits and speak according to their realization. Why, then, do you say that they cannot be spoken of as taking them up?
To sever this doubt, the Sūtra says:
[Sūtra] "Subhūti, what do you think? Can a Stream-enterer have such a thought... (omitted)... he delights in the araṇya?"

That practice. [Treatise] Asaṅga says: From here below is the fifth [section], which concerns the absence of pride during the attainment of excellence through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

Furthermore, among the eight types of abidings, this is the fourth, the abiding free from obstacles. There are twelve obstacles in total: first, pride; second, the absence of pride while having little learning.
Third, although one has heard much, one forms thoughts by grasping at minor objects while practicing the path; ...

up to eleventh, although one possesses the provisions, one does not restrain oneself; twelfth, although one restrains oneself, there is no instruction. The first [case] is for the purpose of abandoning pride.
The Sūtra mentions the *srotāpanna* and so forth; this is intended to demonstrate, by way of their designation, the antidote to the conceit of "I have attained.

That is to say, if those who are *srotāpannas* and so forth entertain the thought that they have attained the fruit, there is the notion of "self," and this notion of self is itself conceit. It does not mean that they are devoid of conceit.

There are four fruits, distinguished by their names and characteristics; this is the explanation of their characteristics. If one demonstrates the absence of pride, it is intended to manifest the act of upholding [the teaching].
To say "in reality there are no dharmas" and so forth is the establishment of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), because in reality there is nothing that proceeds.

This manifests conduct free from contention (*araṇā-caryā*) and the state of one who has abandoned desire; this is for the purpose of making others believe through what one has personally realized, thereby manifesting it.
This is the practice of correspondence (the text erroneously reads "establishing the ultimate meaning"). The verse says:
Because it cannot be grasped and because its own fruit is not grasped when explained, The Sublime One (Sujāta) taught that, based upon that, one is liberated from the two kinds of obscurations.

[The *Huìjiě*] says: "Bodhisattvas take up the lands of those who have attained the fruit;

This refers to the world of birth. However, sentient beings are designated merely by means of the "name-body" (nāmakāya).

This concluding passage is exhaustive. [The old commentary establishes the tenth section below this point.]

(The Tang translation says:)

And yet, while abiding, one does not abide; thus, the principles of subduing and non-subduing are contained therein.

That which gives rise to views is consciousness (*vijñāna*); that which is able to transcend them is wisdom (*jñāna*). Although they differ in depth, their respective names cannot be interchanged.

The prediction of future time; the conduct of Dīpaṃkara was not superior.

This means that "real" (*satya*) has the sense of being non-perverted, and "*tathatā*" has the sense of being non-different and unchanging. Furthermore, the Sūtra says:

To sever this doubt, it is said: "neither real nor unreal. This means there is no falsity because he has attained that bodhi; there is no reality because it does not possess the characteristics of conditioned existence (the characteristics of the five aggregates).

Characteristics. It is not that there are no characteristics of bodhi, because it is not falsely taught. As for "these dharmas are the Buddha-dharmas," this means that all dharmas are Buddha-dharmas;

Because they do not abide in characteristics such as form (*rūpa*), they are not dharmas. Thus, these dharmas which are non-dharmas are themselves the dharmas. ○

The nature of the few dharmas is the essence of unsurpassed bodhi;

Were it not for the Tathāgata’s instruction and transmission, there would be no way to give rise to the subtlety of such realization and entry. Therefore, he turns back to point toward the Dharma possessed by Dīpaṃkara Buddha, asking whether there is any dharma by which one can attain bodhi;

Bestowing a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) serves as the answer; it is simply the ultimate limit of principle. Generally speaking, there are the meanings of phenomena (*dharma*), principle (*li*), cause, and effect.

From the perspective of phenomena, one does not become a Buddha without a prediction; being in the causal stage, one must rely upon teachers and protectors—thus, it may be said that there is a dharma to be attained.
From the perspective of principle, awakening does not depend on others; reaching the fruit, one is called "solely awakened"—thus, it may be said that there is nothing to be attained.
Now, if one seeks an explanation based on the former sense, it would be asked: "Does a dharma exist that attains bodhi?

It is so, it is so. Although these two meanings are both applicable, in principle there is no attainment. Thus, by way of reductio ad absurdum, the conclusion is established:
"If there were dharmas," and so forth. This means that if there were any dharma that could receive the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*), it would not be unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
This would utterly contradict the principle of the one suchness (*tathatā*) and quiescence (*śānti*); it would not be the path for attaining Buddhahood, and thus it is not worth engaging with.
This is a record. By stating that "in reality there are no dharmas," he establishes his argument; yet, as its underlying principle was still not clear, he further provides an explanation by asking:
"Why is this so? Because 'Tathāgata' is the meaning of the suchness (tathatā) of all dharmas. Now, suchness is precisely true suchness (bhūtatathatā).
Because it is true suchness, it is equal. This refers to attaining perfect enlightenment within the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), which is suchness.
How could there be any other dharma that is attained? Therefore, the Treatise says: "Because True Suchness (tathatā) is non-dual. From the words "If someone were to say...
onwards, it repeatedly negates the characteristics of attainment and non-attainment, ultimately resulting in neither reality nor unreality.

Because there is no reality, there is no attainment; because there is no unreality, there is no non-attainment. Furthermore, because there is no reality, it does not possess the characteristics of conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta); because there is no unreality...
It is not that the characteristic of *tathatā* (suchness) is non-existent; therefore it is said that the Tathāgata speaks of all dharmas as equal.
To say that "all dharmas are the Buddha-dharma" means they are not false; to say that "all dharmas are not [ultimately] all dharmas" means they are not real.
That which is neither false nor real is called "all dharmas. These all dharmas are yet again not all dharmas; they are likewise one suchness.
And that is all. As for the verse’s statement regarding the bestowing of a prediction at a later time:

if one were to receive a prediction at a later time and not attain *bodhi* immediately, then one's practice would not be supreme; how then could one reach *bodhi* and receive a prediction? Therefore, the following explanation says:

Thus, their doubt is resolved. As for the claim that there is a discrepancy between the treatise and its commentary, it is likely due to the translator being confused regarding the intent of the verse and failing to master its phrasing; this point especially deserves attention.

How, then, could bodhisattvas resolve their minds to deliver sentient beings and purify buddha-fields? To sever this doubt, it is now divided into two parts.
Doubt. As the Sūtra says:
[Sūtra] "Subhūti, it is as if there were a person whose body was vast and tall... (omitted)... there is no self, no person, no sentient being, and no life-span."

[Śāstra] Asaṅga says: From here below is the seventeenth [topic], which serves as the entry into the path of realization (*praveśa-mārga*). It is presented to demonstrate the attainment of wisdom and the abandonment of pride.

There are two kinds of wisdom attained: first, the wisdom that encompasses the spiritual lineage (*gotra-saṃgrāhaka-jñāna*); second, the wisdom of equality (*samatā-jñāna*). Because of the attainment of this wisdom, one is born into the family of the Tathāgata and is certain to succeed to the Buddha-lineage;
this constitutes the wisdom that encompasses the spiritual lineage. As for the wisdom of equality, it refers to the attainment of [the state of] arrival.
The body and the attainment of the body, because of having attained the ultimate transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*). In this regard, there are five kinds of wisdom of equality:
first, equality regarding coarseness; second, the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*); third, association with abandonment; fourth, association with a mind free from expectation.
Fifth, the equality of the path realized by all Bodhisattvas. Because they have attained this wisdom, they manifest a great body that encompasses all sentient beings;
yet within that body, they establish the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Thus, it is neither self nor other. Therefore, the Sūtra says:

"The Tathāgata speaks of the human body as being large, but it is not a large body," and so forth. This is the attainment of wisdom. How does one abandon pride? The Sūtra states: [...]* *Note: The source text appears to be truncated.*

This means that if one harbors such thoughts, one cannot attain the sublime Great Body (mahākāya). The verse says:
Relying upon that Dharmakāya Buddha, The metaphor of the "Great Body" is thus taught.
Because the body is free from all obscurations and pervades all objects, And because of its qualities and its great essence, It is therefore said to be the Great Body;
yet that which is not a body is itself the body, And for this reason, it is called "non-body."

This, moreover, has two meanings: first, pervading all places; second, because its qualities (*guṇa*) are great. Regarding the terms "qualities," "great essence," and so forth:
"pervading all places" means that True Suchness (*tathatā*) is without differentiation from all phenomena (*dharma*). It is called "non-body" (*akāya*).
This refers to the "body. As the Buddha said in the sutra, that which is not a body is called the "Great Body.
That it is "not a body" means it is devoid of all marks (*nimitta*). That it is the "Great Body" means it is the essence of *tathatā* (suchness).

[The Tang translation is largely the same. Guṇadakṣa continues the preceding passage, saying: "Therefore, the World-Honored One, following the sequence, revealed and clarified this. The sutra says... [and so forth]. This is the "Wondrous Great Body."
