[The *Huìjiě*] says: Because one who possesses the virtues capable of adornment must necessarily have a body that is accomplished, yet because the principle of the *dharmakāya* is ultimate, it should not admit of characteristics that involve dependence or opposition.
This is why the existence or non-existence of the Tathāgata’s marks is difficult to determine.
As clarified above, the fulfillment of merit and wisdom constitutes the virtue capable of adornment; however, the ultimate principle of the *dharmakāya* cannot tolerate the presence of such marks.
Therefore, the Buddha asked Subhūti: "Can the Buddha be seen by means of a body of form endowed with all its marks? He replied, "No.

Asaṅga explains this directly by establishing the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*): thus it is said that what the Tathāgata calls a body of form endowed with all its marks is precisely not a body of form endowed with all its marks;
that which is a mark is precisely no-mark, and that which is no-mark is precisely a mark. This is all there is. (End of section) Tian.
The Master further explains this by resolving doubts, stating in verse: "The Dharma-body is the ultimate essence," and so forth. The intent is no more than this:
the Buddha possesses both a Dharma-body and a form-body (*rūpakāya*). To speak of their essential nature, the Dharma-body is without marks while the form-body has marks.
Yet, when speaking of their identity, the two are not mutually exclusive. This is still an explanation made through conceptual differentiation; from the perspective of ultimate principle, however—
The form-body (*rūpakāya*) is also the Buddha; yet it is neither identical to nor separate from the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
Because they are not identical, there is no duality of marks and signs (*lakṣaṇavyañjana*); because they are not separate, it is not that they are non-existent as two.

Therefore, it is said that [the form-body] is not separate from the dharma-body and so forth. Guṇadatta says: "One perceives the dharma-body by relying upon its physical characteristics (*rūpalakṣaṇa*); that which is not fully complete is the dharma[-body]."
These words exhaust the matter. Thus, that which is adorned by merit and wisdom is the characteristic of the form-body (*rūpakāya*);

that which is ultimately non-existent in principle is the characteristic of the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). Although they are termed "existence" and "non-existence," in principle there is no difference in their ultimate aim.
Although various treatises may differ or agree in their explanations of these meanings, in their general essence there is no distinction.
[Question] Vasubandhu says: Furthermore, there may be doubt as to how it can be said that the Tathāgata preaches the Dharma if the physical marks of the Tathāgata’s body cannot be perceived.
To sever this doubt, [the Sūtra] says:
[Sūtra] Subhūti, do not think that the Tathāgata has such a thought... this is called teaching the Dharma.
[Śāstra] Asaṅga says: From here below is the fifth [section], the perfection of speech; herein, the ultimate truth (paramārtha) is also established.
Therefore, the sūtra says... The verse states:
As with the Buddha, so it is with the Dharma; The two distinctions that have been taught Are not separate from the dharmadhātu;
In teaching the Dharma, there is no intrinsic nature.
Devaśarman’s commentary states: "In order to sever doubts, as in the Sūtra passage: 'If someone were to say that the Tathāgata has preached any Dharma,' etc.
Regarding the verse's mention of "two distinctions," these refer to: first, the Dharma that is preached; and second, the meaning contained therein.

As for the statement that "there is no Dharma that can be preached, yet this is called preaching the Dharma," it means that [the preaching] is not separate from the *dharmadhātu* of *tathatā*. If it were separate, it would have no self-nature.
The characteristics can be explained; therefore, it is said that the teaching of the Dharma has no intrinsic characteristic (*sva-lakṣaṇa*). [The Tang translation is largely the same. Guṇadakṣa says:

Furthermore, if the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), the Buddha’s sphere of experience, and his form-body (*rūpa-kāya*) were all without substance, how could he be endowed with a multitude of virtues?

If even the verbalized characteristic-body (*vākya-lakṣaṇa-kāya*) were likewise non-existent, this doubt would arise. To dispel this, one must ensure that the notion of "having something to say" is definitively eliminated.
Because of this grasping, it is said: "If anyone says that the Tathāgata has taught any dharma," and so forth.

This means that when one speaks of the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), one does not perceive any internal or external phenomena—whether tainted (*sāsrava*) or untainted (*anāsrava*)—that could be truly or substantially taught (Seventeenth [Section on] Severing Doubt).
[The *Huìjiě*] says: "Where there is a body, there is speech; if one were without a body, what speech could there be?
Vasubandhu takes this passage as establishing the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), merely demonstrating that there is no speech at all.
Yet the verse states, 'As it is with the Buddha, so it is with the Dharma. Thus, by analogy with the Buddha, the Dharma likewise cannot be possessed. Nevertheless..."
Regarding the two types of distinctions—the words and the meanings—expounded within the teachings of a single lifetime, what is their nature?
Therefore, it is said that they do not depart from the *dharmadhātu*. This means that although there is verbal expression, it does not depart from the principle of non-expression.

If one were to abandon the *dharmadhātu*, even the self-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the teaching could not be apprehended. Thus, non-expression is itself expression, and expression is itself non-expression.
This is the ultimate way of teaching the Dharma; therefore it is said: "There is no Dharma that can be taught—this is called teaching the Dharma.
Vimalakīrti said: "In the teaching of the Dharma, there is neither speaking nor indicating; in the hearing of the Dharma, there is neither hearing nor attaining.
All of this refers to this very point. Thus, the doubts of clinging to existence and clinging to non-existence are dispelled.

【Doubt】 Vasubandhu said: Furthermore, there may be doubt as to who could believe this teaching if it is said that the Buddhas have no Dharma they preach, and that even the non-separation from the *dharmadhātu* does not exist. To sever this doubt, it is as stated in the Sūtra:

[Sūtra] At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, will there be any sentient beings in future ages who, upon hearing this Dharma being preached, will give rise to faith?
The Buddha said: “Subhūti, they are not sentient beings, yet they are not non-sentient beings. Why is this?
Subhūti, as for what are called ‘sentient beings,’ the Tathāgata has said they are not sentient beings; it is thus.”
[The term] "named sentient beings" (the text is found in the Wei translation).
[Treatise]: Asaṅga says: From here below is the sixth mind, which is fully endowed. Within this, there are further six kinds of purity:

first, the purity of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), up to the sixth, the purity of abiding in the modes of practice (*caryā-vihāra*). Regarding the purity of the foundations of mindfulness, as the Sūtra says, and so forth; this concerns sentient beings.

The middle section demonstrates this by way of the Lord’s application of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*). The statement that "he is neither a sentient being nor a non-sentient being" demonstrates the two truths (*satyadvaya*).
Furthermore, it should also be said: "This person is the foremost among the rare," which demonstrates the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), its uniqueness, and its correspondence. The verse says:
What is taught and the teacher are profound; there are those capable of believing it. It is neither a sentient being nor not a sentient being, neither a noble one nor not a noble one.
Tianqin’s commentary states: If one believes this sutra, that person is neither a sentient being nor not a sentient being, neither...
"Sentient beings" does not refer to ordinary, mundane sentient beings, because they are not devoid of the noble essence (*āryatva*).

Nor does it refer to those who are not sentient beings with the noble essence, because they do possess that noble essence. Therefore, it is said that what is not a sentient being is designated as a "sentient being. (The Tang translation states:
"What is not a sentient being" refers to other [mundane] sentient beings, because they are not endowed with the nature of the noble ones. "What is not a non-sentient being" is due to...)
Because it corresponds to the nature of the noble ones (*ārya*), and because it is contrasted with the nature of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), it is not a sentient being (*sattva*).

Because it is contrasted with the nature of the noble ones, it is not a non-sentient being. Guṇadatta says: Furthermore, in order to demonstrate that those who accept what has been taught are rare, he asks:
"How is it not a sentient being? It is because when one searches for its essence—whether within the aggregates (*skandha*) or apart from the aggregates—it cannot be found.

"It is not that there are no sentient beings," because, according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), they are designated based on the correspondence between the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and the results of karma.
(If this section were added as a separate doubt, there would be eighteen; however, following the Qin edition, it is here treated briefly.)
[The *Huìjiě*] says: "In the old treatise, the presence or absence of sixty-two characters in this sutra refers precisely to this chapter. Now, regarding this text:
its brevity is not a deficiency, and its inclusion is not redundant.

Since what is stated here has already been fully expressed in the preceding text, it is appropriate that it be concise. Nevertheless, in the verses and the commentaries, these [six points] must be understood as being complete within the mind."

Regarding the first point of meaning: if it were omitted, it would be incomplete; therefore, it is appropriate to retain it. However, we now follow the version by Kumārajīva; perhaps there is another intention [behind his choice], so we shall likewise proceed with brevity.

As for Asaṅga’s view that "that which manifests as the World-Honored One’s applications of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) is identical to the pure *tathatā* realized by the Tathāgata—this is their application of mindfulness"—it is because of this that one can generate faith in the sūtras. This differs from...

Regarding all ordinary sentient beings, because they are spoken of according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), they are also sentient beings who are unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) noble ones (*ārya*).
Thus, they are described as "neither not-is nor is," thereby abiding between the state of the ordinary person and the sage.
Other discussions concerning similarities and differences follow their respective meanings accordingly.

【Doubt】 Vasubandhu says: "If the Tathāgata does not obtain even a single dharma called 'Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi,' how can there be a progressive attainment of bodhi through successive stages of superior realization? To sever this doubt, [the Sūtra] says:
[Sūtra] Subhūti said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, that which the Buddha has attained as *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*...
this is called wholesome dharma. [Śāstra] Asaṅga says: From here below is the second [section], for the sake of perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).

Within this, the phrase “there is no dharma” is intended to eliminate the view of existence and thereby reveal both awakening (*bodhi*) and the path to awakening (*bodhimārga*). This revelation is expressed in two ways, namely:
*Anuttara* means "unsurpassed" (*an-uttara*), as it reveals the specific characteristics of *bodhi* and the characteristics of liberation;
therein not even a speck of dust’s worth of a dharma can be found, and thus it is "non-existent.
Next, *samyak-saṃbodhi* means "perfectly equal," as it reveals the characteristic of equality among those who possess *bodhi*; it is by virtue of *bodhi* that this is known. All...
In the Buddha’s ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), there is no high or low; thus, there is no high or low regarding lifespan and so forth.
Furthermore, the statement "because there are no sentient beings" and so on demonstrates that within birth and death (*saṃsāra*), the dharmic characteristic of bodhi is one of equality.
Next, to manifest the path of bodhi, as the sūtra says, "cultivating all wholesome dharmas," etc., those which are not wholesome dharmas are established as the first [category].
Because they share a single characteristic of meaning, the verse says:
In that state, there is not even the slightest dharma; One knows that awakening is unsurpassed. The dharmadhātu neither increases nor decreases;
it is pure, equal, and its own characteristic. It possesses unsurpassed skillful means And is free from all outflowing phenomena (āsrava-dharma).
Therefore, that which is not a pure dharma is itself the dharma of purity. Tianqin’s commentary states:
From here on, the scriptural text is intended to sever doubts; it demonstrates that there is no dharma to be realized, yet this is called "attaining anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
This means that in the state of bodhi, there is not a single dharma that can be realized, as the sūtra says, and so forth. Therefore.
It is called "unsurpassed" (*anuttara*). The verse states that the *dharmadhātu* neither increases nor decreases, and so forth, which explains the meaning of "unsurpassed" through four points.

As the Sūtra says: "This Dharma is equal, without high or low. Because it neither increases nor decreases, it is unsurpassed. Furthermore, because the *dharmakāya* of all Buddhas is pure and there is nothing superior to it, it is unsurpassed.
This is because, being free from selfhood (*nirātman*), one attains the equality of *bodhi*.
It is unsurpassed. Furthermore, because that dharma has the true nature of selflessness as its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), it is unsurpassed.

Regarding "unsurpassed skillful means," this refers to the fulfillment of all wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma*). If other wholesome dharmas for awakening were deficient, the skillful means would be surpassed.
As the sūtra says, "all wholesome dharmas," and so forth. Within that, what are called "non-wholesome dharmas" refer to those...

Because phenomena (*dharma*) are without outflows (*āsrava*). Thus, the verse says, "and free from outflows," and so forth. To say "outflows" means that which is not pure; that which is not an outflow is pure.
This refers precisely to the wholesome phenomena that are definitively without outflows. The Tang translation states:

"If one says that the Tathāgata has no phenomena that are to be realized, how could he be free from subsequent and successive perfect awakenings? It is in this sequence that he is called 'Unsurpassed'."
"Awakening. To answer this doubt, it is stated that only an awakening that is not a dharma of existence is truly called "unsurpassed awakening"; the rest of the text is largely the same.
○ Guṇadakṣiṇa says: "If, in the realm of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), form, body, and speech are all unobtainable..."
"Is the nature of the Dharma-body also like this? To dispel this doubt, the Sūtra says [as follows]:
It means that because the Buddha has realized reality and does not perceive even the slightest dharma as being obtainable, it is called *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Because these dharmas are equal and lack high or low, there is nothing to be obtained. Why are they equal? Because they are devoid of self, person, sentient beings, and so forth.
Just as there is no self in persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*), so too is there no self in phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*); thus, they are equal and non-dual.

By what reason is this principle of non-attainment (*anupalabdhi*) proven? Therefore, it is said that all wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma*) and so forth [exist]. If wholesome dharmas possess substantiality (*svabhāva*), how can they prove the principle of non-attainment?

Therefore it is said: "Wholesome dharmas," which the Tathāgata says are not wholesome dharmas, because in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*) they are of the nature of non-arising and thus unattainable.
To speak of "wholesome dharmas" is a conventional expression (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and not the true meaning. (Chapter 18: Severing Doubts)
[The *Huìjiě*] says: "The body and speech that express what has been realized share one and the same principle.

Because Subhūti understood that what was just expressed by the body was not actually expressed by the body, he raised a series of analogical questions. The Buddha’s response likewise stated, 'In truth, there are no dharmas,' and so forth;
thus, supreme bodhi is attained through non-attainment. If one were to say there is attainment, it would not be equality, nor could it be called 'non-existent' (or 'unattainable')."
Therefore, it is said that "this Dharma is equal, without high or low. This refers to Bodhi, which has no height of Nirvana and no depth of Saṃsāra;
there is no attainment by sages and no non-attainment by ordinary beings.
This speaks of equality based on the nature of reality (li-xing). If we consider it in terms of cultivated virtue, it is not that one does not attain Bodhi through wholesome dharmas; however—
When one is free from views such as a self or a person, then that which is cultivated is devoid of marks; therefore it is said that the Tathāgata speaks of non-dharmas as dharmas.

This also does not contradict the principle of non-attainment. The treatise takes the initial passage as a manifestation of the characteristics of bodhi, clarifying its meaning through two kinds of discourse.
That is to say, by means of the unsurpassed discourse, it manifests the specific characteristic of bodhi and—
The characteristic of liberation is that because not even the slightest dharma can be apprehended, all are unsurpassed.
The expression "equal speech" reveals that both persons and dharmas are equal in relation to bodhi. The subsequent passage serves to demonstrate the path to bodhi.
However, the Path is itself Bodhi. This means that the path to Bodhi is itself the wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma*).
As for the statement that it is not a wholesome dharma, this is also established from the perspective of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

Regarding Vasubandhu’s expression of doubt, saying that one attains Bodhi progressively by departing from those progressively higher realized dharmas: the term "progressively higher" (*uttarottara*) is spoken in relation to what follows; that is, in terms of sequential stages.

To discuss this: one breaks through a portion of delusions and realizes a portion of Bodhi. From the perspective of subsequent stages, this constitutes a progressively superior realization of the Dharma;
yet, from the perspective of the preceding stage looking back at the subsequent, one departs from the progressively superior realization and successively attains later Bodhi.
Although there is thus both departure and attainment, in reality there is no dharma and no realization. This is precisely the intention behind severing doubt. The rest is not [discussed here].
An alternative explanation.

[Doubt]: Vasubandhu says: Furthermore, there is a doubt: "If one attains bodhi by fulfilling all wholesome dharmas, then the dharmas that have been taught would not attain great bodhi, because they are indeterminate (avyākṛta). To sever this doubt, it is as stated in the Sūtra:
[Sūtra] Subhūti, if within a trichiliocosm... [omitted] ...these are called ordinary persons. [Treatise] Asaṅga says:

From here below is the third section, which establishes the Dharma of Great Benefit. Within this, for the purpose of establishing the instruction on the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), the Sūtra states:
"Do not say that the Tathāgata has such a thought," and so forth. This means that if the Tathāgata...
One knows this through its radiance. To speak of "sentient beings" is to entertain the grasping for a self (*ātma-grāha*). In order to abandon this attachment, it is said:
"That which the Tathāgata speaks of as 'having a self' is precisely not having a self. Only the ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) of the Hīnayāna possess such grasping; therefore, it is said:
"That which the Tathāgata speaks of as an 'ordinary person' is precisely not an ordinary person. The verse says:
Although it is said that unconditioned phenomena (avyākṛta-dharma) are taught as its cause, for this reason, the single Jewel of the Dharma surpasses immeasurable worldly treasures.
Its numerical power and excellence are peerless;
likewise, its peerless cause cannot be illustrated by any analogy among all worldly phenomena.

○ Vasubandhu’s commentary states: To sever this doubt, it is said that although the Dharma taught is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), one can nevertheless attain great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*), for without departing from the Dharma taught, enlightenment cannot be attained; therefore, it serves as the cause of enlightenment.
Furthermore, as for the statement that [this] is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), this meaning is not so. You are indeterminate, whereas my Dharma is determinate;

therefore it is said, "one jewel of the Dharma," and so forth. Regarding the phrases "numerical superiority," "power superiority," "incomparable superiority," and "excellence," these mean that compared to the previous merit, this merit is superior.
First is numerical superiority; second is power superiority; third is incomparable superiority—as stated extensively in the sūtras.
Fourth is the superiority of the cause (*hetu-viśeṣa*). This cause is superior to that [other] cause.

(The Tang translation renders *bala-sadṛśa* as "resemblance of power" [*śe-lei*], meaning that just as human power has degrees of strength and weakness, and human types have distinctions of nobility and lowliness, it cannot be compared or enumerated.)
The remainder of the text is largely the same. Guṇadakṣa asks: "For what reason is this further calculation performed?
It is because the minds of practitioners today are now courageous and resolute" (Chapter Nineteen: Severing Doubts).
[The *Huìjiě*] says: Since one establishes the great benefit only after realizing the path of enlightenment, Asaṅga considers this to be the "Dharma for Establishing Great Benefit.
Now, as for the Dharma of great benefit, none surpasses the merit of upholding and expounding this sutra;
therefore, he again cites the merit of giving the seven treasures of a trichiliocosm as a standard of comparison. The text uses the cause to illustrate the effect, which is itself the effect.
The supreme skillful means for transforming and delivering sentient beings are even greater than this.

If the Tathāgata, according to what he knows, were to say that there are sentient beings who are delivered, that would constitute the grasping of a self (*ātma-grāha*). To remain free from attachment, it is said that the Tathāgata teaches that there is no such self;
this is precisely how the instruction established in the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is presented. If...
Maitreyanātha, however, continues to raise a doubt based on the preceding [verse]:

"If one attains bodhi by fulfilling wholesome dharmas, then since the teachings spoken are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), would it not conversely follow that one cannot attain it? To sever this doubt, he cites a verse in response, saying:
"Although speech is indeterminate, it can serve as a cause. This is a response that accords with the question. Furthermore, he says: "You [the teaching] are indeterminate."
This refers to those who are doubtful; because they doubt and cannot reach a decision, it is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). Alternatively, one may say: "You doubt whether this dharma is indeterminate.
If what I have taught is free from characteristics and supremely excellent, how can it be called indeterminate?
This would contradict the question and answer. Furthermore, regarding the verse that says "all worldly dharmas," etc., it is explained by means of the four ultimate meanings (*paramārtha*).
The comparison [of merits] can be understood from the text.
【Doubt】 Vasubandhu said: "Furthermore, there is a doubt: if this Dharma is equal and without high or low, why does the Tathāgata speak of 'delivering sentient beings'?
To sever this doubt, it is as stated in the Sūtra:
[Sūtra] Subhūti, what do you think? Do not say that the Tathāgata is [as previously cited].
[Śāstra] As stated above in the text of Asaṅga, etc. The verse says:
In the equal and true Dharma-realm, the Buddha does not deliver sentient beings. Because names are common to those aggregates, they do not depart from the Dharma-realm;
to grasp at "I" as delivering them is an error. To grasp at those dharmas is to grasp at the delivery of sentient beings;
one should know that non-grasping is true grasping.

The commentary by Vasubandhu states: How does one sever doubt? It means that the conventional designation of "birth" is coextensive with the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), yet it is not separate from the *dharmadhātu*, because there is no differentiation between them.
Therefore, it is called the "equal and true *dharmadhātu*. For this reason, there are no sentient beings to be delivered.
As the Sūtra says, and so forth. The verse states: "To grasp at a self and deliver it is a fault," meaning that if a Tathāgata were to grasp at the five...

To think that there are sentient beings within the aggregates (*skandha*) who are to be saved and brought to liberation, and that "I am the one who can save them," is the fault of grasping at signs (*nimitta-grāha*).
This is because one is attached to those phenomena. Furthermore, the Sūtra says: "The Tathāgata speaks of 'self' and so forth. Thus, the verse says: "Not grasping, yet grasping.

This means that since those [phenomena] are fundamentally unreal, they should not be grasped; yet, failing to grasp what should not be grasped, ordinary beings grasp them and thereby give rise to existence.
This is the meaning of "not grasping while grasping. Even according to the Buddha’s words, it is "grasping while not grasping. One grasps sentient beings as those to be delivered;
it is merely grasping that is non-grasping. Furthermore, the Tathāgata says that ordinary sentient beings are called "non-beings," because they do not give birth to the dharmas of the noble ones.
[The meaning of the Tang translation differs slightly (etc.). Guṇadakṣa said: Furthermore...
Next, there may be doubt that if the Tathāgata says "there are no sentient beings," it contradicts other teachings, such as those in a sūtra which state:
"Immeasurable sentient beings, having obtained me as their spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), are liberated from birth and so forth. To dispel this doubt, the sūtra says [as follows]:

"[There are] no sentient beings" because this is the ultimate truth (paramārtha); furthermore, it is because [the Buddha] embraces them with great compassion (mahākaruṇā) as if they were himself. If...
If there were truly sentient beings distinct from the Tathāgata who were to be delivered, the Tathāgata would possess the grasping of a self (*ātma-grāha*).

This "grasping of a self" is said by the Tathāgata to be "non-grasping. Here, "non" (*a-*) has the sense of being unwholesome (*akuśala*), for it binds sentient beings and causes them to dwell in saṃsāra.
Furthermore, "non" has the sense of lacking intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), because there is neither a grasper nor an object to be grasped; yet ordinary people grasp at it falsely.
It is for the sake of causing them to understand. As the Sūtra says: "Only ignorant ordinary persons [perceive this].
This means that those who have not yet attained the state of a noble one (ārya) each cling to a distinct self, and thus [the self] arises; however, that [self] does not truly arise.

Furthermore, because phenomena arise from conditions and are not created by a self, they are said not to arise. To speak of "arising" is merely to follow conventional worldly discourse (*lokavyavahāra*). (From *Duan yi ershi*)

[The *Huìjiě*] says: Regarding the fact that the text, following the section on comparative evaluation, issues the statement "Do not say [that there is no one to be saved]," it is because the preceding text stated, "Since this Dharma is equal, there is no birth to be saved. It was feared that the assembly might give rise to such a doubt.

Therefore, he stops there with these words. Although Subhūti had not yet spoken, his mind was still undecided; thus, [the Buddha] directly told him that in reality there are no beings to be saved. As the verse says:
"In the equal and true Dharma-realm, the Buddha does not save sentient beings"—this statement is exhaustive.
Now, in the single True Dharma-realm, there is fundamentally neither delusion nor awakening; how, then, could there be such things as "beings" or "Buddhas"? And...

Who is it that can deliver those who are to be delivered? If one were to say that there are sentient beings to be delivered, then the Buddha would necessarily possess views such as a self or a person.
If, however, there is truly no self, it is clear that there are no sentient beings. Yet, the Tathāgata speaks of a self.
Whenever ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) cling to a self, [the Buddha] accords with their delusion and, though there is no self, speaks of a self.

Now, do ordinary beings truly exist as ordinary beings? To speak according to reality, even "ordinary beings" cannot be apprehended. Therefore it is said: "What the Tathāgata calls 'an ordinary being' is not actually an ordinary being;
it is merely designated as 'an ordinary being' in accordance with worldly convention. In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), [there is none]."
Then they do not exist. If one knows that there is no arising yet speaks of arising, this is likewise "crossing over while not crossing over.
This refers to knowing that sentient beings have no inherent existence, yet vowing to deliver those non-existent sentient beings.

Thus, regarding whether sentient beings exist or not, and whether the Tathāgata delivers them or not—each has its own underlying principle; it is only when one grasps at them as substantial that it is otherwise.

【Doubt】 Vasubandhu said: Furthermore, there is another doubt. Although one cannot perceive the Tathāgata through his marks because they are not the essence of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body, the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body is nevertheless known by means of comparison with physical marks;
thus, the Tathāgata is also accomplished through marks of merit. To sever this doubt, [the text] says as in the Sūtra:
[Sūtra] Subhūti, what do you think? Can the Tathāgata be perceived by means of the thirty-two marks? [The Buddha said:
It is not by means of the perfection of marks that the Tathāgata has attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
[Śāstra] Asaṅga says: From here below, the fourth section is for the purpose of encompassing the *dharmakāya*. Within this, the first verse demonstrates how [the Buddha] should not be viewed;
because he cannot be seen, those who act in this way are said to follow a false path, and are thus called "those of false tranquility."

Because those who have attained *dhyāna* are called "tranquil," *dhyāna* is termed "contemplative cultivation" (*bhāvanā*). "Contemplation" (*cintā*) is subsumed under the mental faculty (*manas*), and "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*) is subsumed under consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Because it is subsumed by consciousness and discernment, it cannot be seen; furthermore, all such views belong to the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
The next verse says: "That wondrous body of the Tathāgata is the Dharma-body of all Buddhas. The essence of the Dharma cannot be seen, for that consciousness is unable [to perceive it]."
[He] knows. He then demonstrates that which should not be seen and the conditions by which it should not be seen. Among these, the first two phrases mean that one should see [it] through the Dharma.
"Buddha-Dharma" has the meaning of *tathatā* (suchness). Because it takes the Dharma as its body and suchness as its condition, it gives rise to the Buddha-dharmakāya;
therefore, it cannot be seen. The subsequent two phrases state that it should not be seen due to conditions. Because of that...

Because the Dharma is the characteristic of *tathatā* (suchness), it is not something known through verbal expression; it can only be personally realized (*pratyātma-vedya*). One who perceives reality is able to know it;

therefore, it is said that "the essence of the Dharma is invisible," and so forth. Although one should not perceive it by way of characteristics (*nimitta*), might one attain *bodhi* by taking these as causes?
To dispel such attachment, the Sūtra states: "The Tathāgata can be [perceived] through the perfection of the marks," and so on. Thus, in order to abandon this clinging, it says:

Furthermore, it says, "Do not entertain such thoughts," and so forth. This clarifies that marks (*lakṣaṇa*) are not *bodhi*, nor are they its causal marks, because they are of the nature of form (*rūpa*). The verse states:
The Tathāgata cannot be known through comparison with a body of formal marks; All Buddhas are solely the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
The Wheel-Turning King is not the Buddha; He is not the fruition of the marks and signs. Relying on the accomplishment of merit and virtue, he attains the true Dharma-body;
Because his skillful means differ from [worldly] characteristics, Those who see only form and hear only sound do not know the Buddha.
For the Tathāgata-Dharmakāya Is not within the sphere of consciousness.
○ Vasubandhu’s commentary states: The following is for the purpose of severing doubts.

That is to say, if someone were to claim that merit can produce the marks of a Buddha, and that one thereby attains bodhi through these marks, then it would follow that a universal monarch (cakravartin) must be a Tathāgata.

Therefore, one should know that the Buddha-body cannot be perceived through marks (*lakṣaṇa*). This statement—that it is not the fruit of retribution consisting of the primary and secondary marks—clarifies that the fruit of marks is not accomplished by means of merit (*puṇya*);
rather, it is attained through the distinct characteristics of the skillful means of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).

That is to say, the Dharma-body is the body of the characteristic of wisdom (*jñānalakṣaṇakāya*), and not that body of distinct characteristics produced by merit. If one perceives only form or hears only sound, this is...
Because people do not know that the *tathatā*-dharma-body is not within the realm of consciousness, it is said that "to see forms and hear sounds is to practice a deviant path.
Thus, [the text] says, "That wondrous body of the Tathāgata," and so forth. The Tang translation is largely the same.

Guṇadakṣa says: Because sentient beings mostly give rise to grasping and attachment toward the Buddha’s dharma-body, he speaks of the form-body (*rūpakāya*) as being without intrinsic nature. Furthermore—
In order to cause one to perceive the Dharma-body within the form-body, the verse says: [and so forth].

That is to say, those who claim to see the Buddha merely by seeing the marks and signs of radiance, or by hearing and receiving the words and letters of the sutra-dharma, are told that they are practicing a deviant path;
for the nature of form and sound is not ultimate reality. If so, how then does one see? Therefore, the verse states:
It is said that the Dharma of the Tathāgata constitutes his body; one should simply contemplate the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
This nature of phenomena is not an object of vision, nor can it be known by them. The nature of phenomena refers to emptiness, the absence of intrinsic nature, the absence of arising, and so forth.

This is the first principle body (*paramārthakāya*) of all Buddhas. To see this is called seeing the Buddha. Furthermore, other sūtras state that the vision free from grasping is [the vision of the Buddha].
This is called "seeing the Buddha. Now, regarding the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), it is not something to be grasped through attachment.
Because one realizes the nature of phenomena with a mind of pure wisdom, the nature of phenomena is not an object of sight. Since it is not an object of sight, wisdom cannot know it as an object.
As a sutra says: "The nature of all phenomena is like space; it serves as the basis for all things, yet its essential nature does not exist."

Things are not non-existent things; they are quiescent and devoid of cognition. This is called "knowing," and the one who knows is designated as such according to conventional discourse (The Twenty-first Severance of Doubt).
[The *Huìjiě*] says: The scripture states that the Tathāgata can be seen by means of physical marks (*lakṣaṇa*). This occurs four times in total throughout the preceding and following sections.
Each instance has its own specific purpose based on the distinctions in the arising of the text and the severing of doubts.

The previous instances simply stated that he "cannot be seen"; this one alone speaks of "contemplating" (*guan*). Therefore, as it stands between the possibilities of "yes" and "no," it says: "... Indeed, [the distinction lies between] contemplating and...
Because they perceive differences, there is giving and taking away. This may be said when viewing through principle (*li*), but it is not permissible when viewing through characteristics (*xiang*).
For instance, it is said that the color of a single speck of dust is entirely equal to principle; how much more so, then, is the physical form of sixteen feet surely the Dharma-body?
Yet, when questioned regarding its characteristics, one again says it is not. This is perhaps because those who do not observe well might once again become stuck in characteristics.
[The Master] saw this and therefore again prohibited it. Regarding the fact that the Wei translation adds the final four lines while the Qin version omits them:
from our current perspective, the reasoning of the Wei translation is correct; yet the intent of the Qin version is profound. Each has its own purpose, and it is not easy to judge which is superior.

However, between a text that is sufficient in principle and exhaustive in meaning, and one that is profound in intent and leaves room for further interpretation—which is better? This is what is meant by "merely prohibiting what is erroneous."
It does not state what is correct; the original Qin translation has captured this.
Asaṅga considers it to be the "appropriation of the dharmakāya," implying that the dharmakāya resides precisely where there is no [objective] locus.

Vasubandhu, however, maintains that because it severs doubt, one does not perceive the Tathāgata through physical marks (rūpalakṣaṇa), but regards only suchness (tathatā) as the Tathāgata. This, too, remains a statement of conceptual discrimination.
If the three bodies are perfectly complete, then the form-body and the dharma-body are neither identical nor different; they are neither localized nor non-localized.
How could one possibly speak of them as being separated in such a manner? As discussed by Guṇadeva, this may indeed be called knowing the way of the Buddha’s manifestation.
【Doubt】 Vasubandhu said: There are those who give rise to such a thought:

"If one does not rely on merit to attain great enlightenment, then these bodhisattvas would lose both their merit and the great fruit of retribution. To sever this doubt, it is as stated in the Sūtra:
[Sūtra] Subhūti, if you should think that the Tathāgata does not attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* by means of the marks of perfection...
(therefore it is said that he does not accept merit). [Note: Regarding the phrase "without attachment," Vasubandhu connects this section with the preceding passage.]
[Śāstra] Asaṅga says: From here below is the fifth [section], concerning non-abiding in either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa.

Therefore it is said, "Regarding phenomena, one does not speak of their annihilation. This means that while thoroughly penetrating the phenomena as they abide, one does not sever any of the reflections of saṃsāra;
yet, within nirvāṇa, one acts with mastery for the sake of benefiting sentient beings. This negates a state of exclusive tranquility, and thus it is revealed.

One does not abide in nirvāṇa. If one were to abide in nirvāṇa, one would have to undergo saṃsāra; in order to eliminate this attachment, it is shown that one does not abide in the cycle of existence.
Thus, the Sūtra says that one practices giving with the seven treasures and so forth.

Within this, the statement "knowing all dharmas are without self and thereby accomplishing patience" means that because one has attained mastery over conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), there is no longer that [bondage of] saṃsāra.

Furthermore, it is not produced by the power of karma or afflictions; therefore, it is called "attaining patience through the non-apprehension of self. The merit thus produced is far superior to that [of the former].
When it is said that a bodhisattva does not take up merit, this precisely demonstrates their non-abiding in saṃsāra; for if one were to abide in saṃsāra, one would indeed receive merit.
Moreover, regarding the statement that they do not take up merit, the Buddha has stated elsewhere that one should accept merit.
Because of virtue, and because it is taught through skillful means, one accepts [the teaching] but does not grasp it. To "accept" means to say that [phenomena] exist;
to "grasp" means to cultivate that path. Just as one should not be attached to the accumulation of merit or its fruits, so too here. The verse says:
Not losing the cause of merit and its supreme retribution, Attaining supreme patience and not losing it, thereby obtaining the fruit free from defilement;
Manifesting the marks of supreme merit and virtue— For this reason, the analogy is taught:
this merit has no [further] retribution, And thus one experiences it without grasping.
○ Vasubandhu’s commentary states: From here below, [the text] is intended to sever doubts.

That is to say, although one does not rely on merit to attain true bodhi, one does not lose that merit nor its karmic retribution, because of the ability to achieve the two adornments of merit and wisdom.
Regarding the statement "attaining supreme patience and not losing [merit]," it means that if someone were to think: "The Bodhisattva, having attained non-arising, has lost that merit..."

"Virtue" (guṇa) is mentioned here to prevent [the misconception that merit is lost]; it demonstrates that one does not lose [merit] but rather attains a superior retribution. Therefore, it is said to "demonstrate superior merit and its characteristics.
As the Sūtra states: "Regarding phenomena, do not speak of the characteristic of annihilation.

To say that "one knows all phenomena are without self and attains the patience of non-arising" refers to the two kinds of selflessness; because one attains the two kinds of non-arising characteristics, this merit has no [further] retribution.
This means there is no such retribution for outflows (*āsrava*). Thus, regarding "accepting without grasping":

one accepts because one has obtained retribution for outflows, yet does not grasp it because outflows are subject to censure. (The Tang translation says: "If one says that merit does not realize *bodhi*...")
In that case, the fruit of the Bodhisattva’s merit would have to be severed. To explain this, the verse says: "That merit is not lost," and so forth;
the rest of the text is largely the same. ○ Guṇasāgara said: "If even wisdom cannot know the *dharmatā*, how then does the Buddha realize *bodhi* by means of the perfected marks?
To dispel this doubt, the Sūtra says [the following], thereby revealing the Dharma.

This is because it is the meaning of the characteristics of the *dhātu*. If the establishment of characteristics were the ultimate reality, then the cessation of those characteristics would be called "annihilation.

Yet, there is no Bodhisattva who perceives the annihilation of phenomena; for where there is arising, there is annihilation. If all phenomena are by nature non-arising, then being free from the extremes of annihilation and permanence is the characteristic of the *dharmadhātu*.
One who can have faith and understanding in this gains greater merit than that of giving. As it is said in a verse:
It is said: If a person upholds the True Dharma and gives rise to the bodhicitta, it is not worth even a sixteenth part of understanding emptiness.
Or, regarding the thought that "all phenomena are unarisen," why is this so? Because merit arises.

Although the sutra states that one should not grasp at merit—meaning that in the ultimate sense (paramārtha) there is no merit to be grasped—nevertheless, although it cannot be grasped, merit should [be cultivated].
"Perfected. Because it does not depart from the two truths... (and so forth, up to the twenty-second section on severing doubts). The *Huìjiě* states:
"Regarding the opening text of this section, following the explanation provided by Wúzhù above, it should have stated:
'Because it possesses the marks of fulfillment, one attains bodhi. The Tathāgata rejected this and instead reversed the statement; therefore, he said, 'Not by means of... etc.
There appears to be an extra character "bù" (不) above the word "duō" (多). If one follows Vasubandhu’s commentary, then it would not be "many. Each interpretation has its own significance;

thus, it may be acceptable to preserve both. However, Asanga takes the phrase "not teaching annihilation" (*pradhvaṃsa*) below as meaning "not abiding in either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa," asserting that if one were to generate the mind [of awakening] by exclusively teaching the annihilation of all phenomena, it would seem to fall into the quiescence of nirvāṇa.

This is the view of [clinging to] tranquility. To refute this view, it is said that one penetrates the fact that the reflections of birth and death are not severed, yet through the skillful means of nirvāṇa, one benefits sentient beings; thus, one does not abide in nirvāṇa.

If it were said that practicing generosity implies being attached to the conditioned phenomena of birth and death, then to refute such attachment, it is said: "If a person knows that all dharmas are non-existent..."
I have attained the perfection of patience and gained mastery over conditioned phenomena; thus, I do not abide in saṃsāra.
Precisely because I do not abide in saṃsāra, I am able to emerge from life and enter into death; precisely because I do not abide in nirvāṇa.

This is why they are able to dwell securely in *nirvāṇa*. Although these two forms of non-dwelling exist within the Tathāgata, they are spoken of in terms of the bodhisattva because the cause is manifested through the fruit, and the fruit is used to indicate the cause.

Furthermore, as for the fact that their superior and inferior merit do not reach one another, it is due to the difference between accepting and not accepting [merit]; hence it is said, "Because all bodhisattvas do not accept merit," and so forth. However...
According to other texts, there are cases where one accepts but does not grasp; thus, acceptance (*upādāna*) and grasping (*parigraha*) are distinct, as analyzed in various treatises.
If, however, one follows the present version, since non-acceptance is itself non-grasping, there is an absolute absence of attachment.

This is what is meant by the statement that one should not be attached to either the mass of merit or its fruit. Thus, although the text does not explicitly mention "merit" (*puṇya*), [the principle remains the same].

One attains bodhi, yet does not speak of the annihilation of all phenomena. Although one does not abandon the marks of merit, one speaks of the non-apprehension of a self in phenomena and the attainment of patience as supreme.
Thus, the two adornments of merit and wisdom are accomplished precisely because both abide nowhere.
[Question] Vasubandhu says: If bodhisattvas do not receive karmic retribution, how is it that sentient beings enjoy the merit of those bodhisattvas? As the sūtra states:
[Sūtra] Subhūti, if someone were to say that the Tathāgata comes or goes—and so forth—it is for this reason he is called the Tathāgata. [Śāstra] Asaṅga says:
From here below is the sixth [section], the purity of conduct and dwelling (*caryā-vihāra-śuddhi*). This further has three types: first, conduct and dwelling in the deportments (*īryāpatha*);

second, conduct and dwelling in mastery through the contemplation and destruction of name-and-form (*nāma-rūpa*); and third, conduct and dwelling in non-attachment (*asaṅga*). Regarding conduct and dwelling in the deportments:
The Sūtra says, "Whether coming or going," and so forth. "Activity" refers to going and coming; "abiding" refers to other modes of conduct. The verse states:
This meritorious retribution Is for the sake of transforming all sentient beings.
Spontaneously, through such karma, the Buddhas appear throughout the ten directions. The Buddhas who manifest as transformation bodies come and go, Yet the Tathāgata is eternally unmoving.
Thus, within the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), it is neither one nor different.
Tianqin’s commentary states: This means that while the transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) of all Buddhas possess functional utility, their *dharmakāya* neither comes nor goes.
Therefore, it is said that such karma is spontaneous (*svabhāva*). It is also said that the transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) of the Buddhas come and go;

this is intended to clarify that [the Tathāgata] neither comes nor goes, as stated in various sūtras. If the Tathāgata were subject to the distinction of coming and going, one could not say that he dwells eternally in suchness.
To dwell in suchness means to be unchanging and undifferentiated. (The Tang translation is largely the same.)
Guṇaprabha said: "If, in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), there is no merit to be acquired, why do other sūtras speak of the Tathāgata’s accumulations of merit and wisdom?
To dispel this doubt, it is said [in the following passage]:
Nirvāṇa has no real location, yet reaching it is termed 'going. The same applies to saṃsāra; emerging from it is termed 'coming out.'"
"Come! Not coming and not going is the meaning of Tathāgata. By this, he reveals non-abiding nirvāṇa.

Although there is neither identity nor difference between saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, he draws analogies from within the triple world to lead sentient beings and bring them benefit (Dispelling Doubts, Twenty-three).
[The *Huìjiě*] says: This is explained according to the present passage. It reveals that the Tathāgata’s manifested transformation (*nirmāṇakāya*) is itself the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
Therefore, regarding going and coming, there is no trace of going or coming; regarding walking and staying, one does not perceive the marks of walking or staying.

This is why he is named the Dharma-body Tathāgata. As for Vasubandhu’s [Vasubandhu’s commentary on the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*] taking "walking and staying" to mean purity, it is because [the Dharma-body] is entirely...

Because the Dharma is responsive, whether in motion or at rest, there is nothing that is not pure. According to Vasubandhu’s reliance on his predecessors to sever doubts, that which is moved by merit is the "responsive transformation" (nirmāṇa).
Because it is a responsive transformation, it possesses coming and going; those who do not understand this claim that there is actual coming and going.
This is due to their failure to understand that the Dharma-body is essentially without coming or going.
Furthermore, it is said that the Tathāgata comes from nowhere; this refers to coming from within the true suchness (tathatā) and the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi).
It is also said that he comes by riding the path of reality (yathābhūta-mārga) to achieve perfect enlightenment. Thus, both cultivation and nature, cause and fruit, all rely upon the single suchness.
Because suchness has no coming or going, that which comes from nowhere likewise has no place to go; yet, for the sake of conventional expression, one speaks of "coming."

"Coming" signifies the meaning of following transformation; "going" signifies the meaning of returning to the root. If one speaks of "coming as suchness," this refers to the Tathāgata’s coming as suchness at the twin śāla trees.
Furthermore, that which has no place from which it arises is named the Tathāgata. Thus, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states:
"As for 'coming,' there is nowhere from which it comes," and so forth—all of which expresses this principle. Other treatises discuss this in relation to saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.
"To say there is neither coming nor going" also means there is no discourse regarding spatial direction.
[Doubt] This section below raises one doubt; although there is no explicit text in the treatise [addressing it], according to Guṇadakṣa: "Furthermore, as for the doubt:
if there is neither coming nor going because saṃsāra and nirvāṇa cannot be apprehended, how could the Tathāgata be like Mount Sumeru?"
...and so forth. [The question is: "Do they abide as a collection or a composite? This is to dispel the view that within these many *sattvas* there exists a single composite entity.
As the Sūtra says: [Sūtra] "Subhūti, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family, with a trichiliocosm... (omitted)... this.

This is called the characteristic of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*). [Treatise] Asaṅga says: From here below is the second section, intended to refute the autonomous movement and abiding of the body of name-and-form (*nāmarūpakāya*).

Within this, there are two kinds of skillful means (*upāya*). The refutation of the body of form (*rūpakāya*) is as previously explained; regarding the Buddha, he does not say that he is a collection of atoms (*paramāṇusaṃghāta*).

This means that because the substance of an aggregate is not established, it is called "non-aggregate. If this were not the case, even without being stated, one would naturally know it to have the meaning of an aggregate;
why then would the Buddha need to state it? As the Sūtra says: "The Tathāgata speaks of the world as non-world."
This uses the skillful means of non-perception to dismantle the "name-body" (nāmakāya), namely, because of the world of sentient beings.
Furthermore, when it says that if the world were real, it would be a "unified mass" (piṇḍagraha), this refers to both types of grasping at a mass, as both the realm and its atoms are being discussed.
This means that a "single grasping" refers to taking the category of sentient beings and the world as a single existence.

"Differential grasping" refers to grasping the distinct characteristics of the various aggregations of atoms. The statement that it is "not a single composite characteristic" is for the purpose of establishing the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Furthermore, the phrase "that which is ineffable," etc., means that it exists by way of worldly conventional expression (*vyavahāra*).

They grasp it by way of a solid mass. In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), that phenomenon cannot be described; yet the ordinary beings of the Hīnayāna grasp it according to verbal expression, which is not the ultimate sense.
When the Sūtra says, "The Buddha taught the view of a self," it demonstrates that which is non-conceptualized as it truly is.
This means that what non-Buddhists call the "self," the Tathāgata calls the "view of self. Furthermore, he says that this view of self exists; it is subsumed under [false] views.

For this reason, he establishes the doctrine of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*). When one observes in this way and enters samādhi, one no longer engages in conceptual discrimination;

this is the skillful means of correspondence (*yoga-upāya*). As for the statement regarding the arousal of the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, it is shown for the sake of those who are free from discrimination.

Regarding "all phenomena," this indicates the non-conceptual nature of phenomena. Likewise, "knowledge and vision" and so forth indicate that both the higher mind (*adhicitta*) and wisdom (*jñāna*) are entirely non-conceptual;
therefore, they are knowledge, vision, and resolute conviction (*adhimukti*). This means that because one relies on wisdom through *śamatha*, it is called "knowledge";
because one relies on *vipaśyanā*, it is called "vision. These two rely upon *samādhi*, which is the mastery of internal liberation.

Because it takes mental images as its object, it is called "resolute belief" (*adhimokṣa*). [In the first two stages, the names are translated as] *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, whereby one can know and see. In the third stage, fearing that it might be taken as synonymous with meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the term *samāpatti* is used.

According to the *Awakening of Faith* (*Yuanjue jing*), the first is named *śamatha*, the second is named *samāpatti*, and the third is named *dhyāna*. Now, the current names differ from those; they are identical to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, where the third is collectively named *upekṣā*.

The present use of the term *samāpatti* involves a shift in terminology and definition, resulting in different renderings. When it says, "one who thus believes and resolves does not dwell in the marks of phenomena," this precisely reveals the absence of differentiation.
Another interpretation: within the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), it demonstrates the meanings of non-commonality and association, as previously explained (etc.).
The verse says:
"The world reduced to subtle atoms— This metaphor illustrates that meaning; The subtle atoms are further crushed to powder."
The manifestation of the exhaustion of afflictions is not a collection because it is not accumulated;
it is not merely a single metaphor, nor is it a place of gathering, nor is it a metaphor of differentiation. It is only through following sounds that ordinary beings grasp at perversity;
it is not by attaining non-duality that one finds the Way, for it is far removed from self and dharmas.
To see [the self] is itself non-seeing; it is a false vision lacking reality. This is a subtle obstacle;
by seeing True Suchness (tathatā), one becomes detached from it. Through the two knowledges and samādhi, one thus attains detachment. Tianqin’s commentary states:

Regarding the metaphor of crushing dust into particles, it means that the locus of the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) of True Suchness is neither identical nor different [from its manifestations]. As [it is said]:
They come and abide in that realm of the Dharma; therefore, this analogy is taught to demonstrate that the exhaustion of afflictions (*kleśa*) manifests as neither identical nor different.
It is said that they do not "accumulate" because they are not a collection, and so forth.

This means that, just as when dust is ground into powder, there is no substance that has been gathered such that it could abide in a single location, yet because no distinct locations can be found for those particles, they do not abide in separate places either. In this way, one is far removed from afflictions.
The afflictions and hindrances are exhausted; he abides in that state which is neither one nor many. Furthermore, regarding the metaphor of the world as a "unified mass" (*ekapiṇḍa-lakṣaṇa*):
if there were truly a collection of things, the Tathāgata would not speak of a "collection of atoms. If there were truly a world, the Buddha would not say that the trichiliocosm is a unified mass.
This is because such a collection has no substance that can be grasped; it is merely [the perception] of ordinary beings.
To falsely grasp at things as existing when they do not truly exist is to know them as false; therefore, it is said that "a unified aggregate" is "inexpressible," and so forth.
Furthermore, when the Buddha speaks of the "view of self" and so on, he means that although there is fundamentally no self, one follows words and becomes attached, reckoning them as two views;
thus, it is said that these are merely following sounds and so on, and do not pertain to the absence of self or to dharmas. If one is free from these two...
One immediately attains bodhi. Therefore, the verse further states: "Distant from the view of self and so forth. Regarding "one who sees the self does not see":
this means that one who perceives a self does not perceive that non-self, because there is no real self; it is merely a false conceptualization, for there is no self.
Thus the Tathāgata has taught that the view of a self is such. Seeing dharmas is likewise. As the Sūtra says regarding all...
"One should know the Dharma in this way," and so forth. This means that if one perceives the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), one does not perceive [their true] characteristics.

Therefore, both the perception of a self and the perception of phenomena are non-perceptions; this constitutes a subtle obscuration. If one does not perceive those two, one perceives the Dharma and thereby achieves detachment.

Hence, it is said that "one sees True Suchness (*tathatā*) and becomes detached. Furthermore, the phrase "knowing in this way" and so forth demonstrates that mundane wisdom (*laukikajñāna*) is supreme.
The wisdom of meaning (*arthajñāna*). Furthermore, because one attains detachment from those obstacles by relying on samādhi. [The Tang translation is largely the same. Guṇadakṣa states:
"In this context, 'the multitude of atoms' refers to the elimination of the view of a partless unity; 'not the multitude of atoms' refers to..."
"To dispel the view of a single composite whole, it is said that 'what is called a multitude of atoms is not a thing with parts, yet it is spoken of as a multitude.
Furthermore, to dispel the view of accumulation, it is further stated: 'The Tathāgata says that a world is indeed not a world.

Or again, there are [passages] concerning advancing and retreating (and so forth). Now, it is said that the methods for circulation are manifold:
there are those that constitute an entrustment; those that exhort one to uphold [the teaching]; those that evaluate its merit; those that demonstrate the proper procedures;

those that request the title and summarize the essentials; those that conclude with a summary of benefits following the sutra; those that accord with the preferences of various objects or vehicles; and those that inspire...
Regarding the "vow to widely protect," the passages such as "those who believe, accept, and practice" all pertain to the circulation [of the teaching].
If one follows this intent, then from the point "Subhūti, those who have resolved their minds toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*" downward, it fully contains the meaning of circulation.
As for the statement "one should thus know all phenomena," this constitutes the entrustment.

This is the dissemination [of the teaching]. It causes such understanding and realization. This may be stated according to the extensive text, or it may refer generally to what is taught throughout the entire sutra;
moreover, since the phrase "arousing the mind" is identical to the initial text, one knows that it correctly and universally penetrates this single principle.
Next, the passage beginning with "If there are people who... compares the excellence of their merit and encourages them to uphold [the teaching].

The passage beginning with "How should one expound it for others... demonstrates the method for upholding and explaining it. The section following "When the Buddha had spoken this sutra" indicates that they practiced according to what was taught.

These words of joy constitute one of the four *siddhāntas* (purposes); in general, all [four] are present, as they all give rise to joy. This concludes the request for the title and the summary of the essentials.
Furthermore, this was seen in the preceding text; the remainder should also be complete, though the text is merely abbreviated.

Nevertheless, that this sutra has been handed down to future generations so that its circulation remains unobstructed and its practice of receiving and upholding is particularly flourishing—could this not be because the merit of comparing the beginning and end of this single sutra is profound, and it was entrusted with such earnest diligence?
It must be due to the power of the secret assistance of Prajñā and the depth of the seeds within sentient beings.
For this reason, although some may uphold the sutras for the sake of profit, I have not seen them truly able to uphold them.
Only by not upholding the sutras for the sake of profit can one perhaps realize the Tathāgata’s intent for their circulation. Readers should honor and put this into practice.

I, a fool, began composing this work in the year Jihai. I first drafted it at a forest hermitage by East Lake, arranging its structural order there;
it remained in a chest for nearly twenty years. Then, in the year Yimao, I was honored with the seat of the Patriarch at South Lake.
In the summer of the Wu-wu year, my foot ailment subsided slightly, allowing me to edit and finalize these works into four volumes, thereby fulfilling my long-held aspiration.

Shortly thereafter, I received the command from Mount Zhu Peak; the assembly requested their publication, and as the remaining four sutra blocks were prepared in sequence, they were finally ready for carving.
